utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. Colonel, if I could remind you of the affirmation which you took when your evidence commenced, that still applies. Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Good morning, Colonel. Colonel -- I'm getting a lot of feedback in here. Colonel Nesic, can you hear me okay? Colonel, I'm sorry for the disruption. Are you able to hear me?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Colonel, your unit on the 6th of December on Zarkovica was the only unit that had Maljutkas and recoilless guns. Is that correct? Of the units under the command of the 2nd Operational Group, it was the only unit that had Maljutkas and recoilless guns?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of all the units deployed at Zarkovica on that day, only my unit had those pieces that you mentioned. If there were any other units under the command of the 2nd Operational Group that had those weapons, that is a question that I can't answer. As we said before, the operational group covered a large area, and many units were deployed there. Therefore, I can't talk about all those units.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Colonel, we're narrowing it -- sorry, the sound system is not good today. We are narrowing it just to Zarkovica on the 6th of December. You were the only unit that had those weapons, and that was your answer. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. My unit was not the only unit that had those weapons. In the infantry companies, they also had recoilless guns.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The Maljutkas were exclusively with your unit, though. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically anti-armour wire-guided missiles, 9K-11, yes my unit had those.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. I'm sorry about having to speak rather low, but I'm getting a terrible feedback and you may be getting the same.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: There is simply too much feedback to work on like this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I am advised that one possible source of the problem is an interplay between your earphones and your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I was also so advised. I'll try to step back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Perhaps you shall --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Stand straight like my mother said.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Colonel, can you hear me okay without blowing your eardrums out?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't hear you at all. All I can hear is the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Interpreters, is it clear now?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We suppose so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your testimony yesterday indicated that you had a constant observation of activities in the areas that you could see from Zarkovica, and you indicated that you could see a great deal, including virtually all of the Old Town. Now, on the 2nd of December and on the 4th of December and on the 5th of December, I'm going to show you from P66 a video that is in evidence before this Chamber. We would like to take the 2nd of December -- what was happening on the 2nd of December. On the 2nd of December, you also had constant observation. That would not be different from any other day, would it? Colonel?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you have me in mind specifically, that wasn't the case because at one point in time, as far as combat operations were concerned, well, I, too, was observing. But if you mean uninterrupted observation of that area, yes, it was uninterrupted. There was uninterrupted observation. There was an observer who was at the position all the time, and he kept observing and noting down all the important details that were observed in Dubrovnik and the general area. And he would report on those.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, we'll be looking at 28.58 through 29.22 for the 2nd of December, if we may see it, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Is your screen showing you a gathering of people?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, are we having difficulty with Sanction?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Had you seen -- did your screen show you -- I'm having difficulty over here. Had your screen shown you a gathering of persons now? No. Okay, it is not --

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you can't see anything. The screen is blank. There's no image whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Sorry. We seem to be having technical difficulties today. We will try again. We're showing no signal so apparently -- Your Honours, are you having any luck either?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We have the same amount of nothing as you. Now here we are.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: There's a something.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: This is the 2nd of December 1991. I would like to ask to take it to the frame where the festival or gathering in the Old Town of Dubrovnik. You see older people and children, women.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Now, this view was also the view from Zarkovica. Did your observers, your 24-hour observers, report to you that there were civilians in the square at Zarkovica -- I'm sorry, at the Old Town? Was that confirmed to you, sent up the chain?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Madam, this sort of information, civilians moving about, was not important for us. We did not monitor civilians moving about. Our job was to notice military targets moving about. After all, civilians were moving about Dubrovnik and the Old Town on a daily basis. Therefore, we did observe them moving about, but they were not of relevance to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: May I ask, please, the next frame, which is, Madam Case Manager, December 4th between 29.48 and 30.13.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: This is in the Old Town. This is Mr. Bernard Kouchner who was visiting the Old Town, and there are human beings on the street, old ladies, young ladies, people in civilian clothing. Was it reported to you by your observers that this activity was taking place in the Old Town, that there were civilians on the 4th of December?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Madam. Nothing special was said about that. But as I've already said, we noticed people there on a daily basis, even more massive gatherings in the Old Town, and not small groups like this one. But then again, I must say, this was of no relevance to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If we can move on, please, to the 5th of December. The frame would be 30.14 through 30.40.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: This is a concert in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see anything really.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Let's see as it moves on. Perhaps it gets a little better. You certainly could hear, could you not, music emanating from the area that was less than 2 kilometres or approximately 2 kilometres from your positions? You could hear music, couldn't you? There's evidence before this Court that music emanating from your positions was audible.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I couldn't hear any music now. I had no sound in my earphones. Secondly, that music could not be heard at Zarkovica. As far as I have been able to observe since the image was very dark and blurred, this is inside a building. And I think it would have been quite impossible for any of those sounds in Dubrovnik to be heard at Zarkovica. For that, you would have needed a really good PA system to play the music so it could be heard that far away.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you have reports of people coming and going to a festivity on the 5th of December? Was that reported by your observers? By people, I mean civilians coming and going to enjoy a music festival on the 5th of December?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, first of all, I would have been supposed to know that there was a festivity going on in a certain hall. I should have tasked the observer to monitor that particular building, and then he could have reported back to me whether 15, 20 or whatever people had assembled there, what they were wearing, tuxedos or jeans; that sort of thing. But as I said before, civilians were moving about the Old Town and the Stradun on a daily basis, and this was observed every day. But that was of no military relevance to us, people walking about the Old Town. We didn't record data on that because that was not important. None of those people put us at risk. Why, then, would I be paying special attention to a handful of civilians moving about a street and people going about their own business?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And you would agree that civilians were moving about and minding their own business on the 6th of December as well in the Old Town of Dubrovnik by the logic of what you have just said. Isn't that correct? That there were civilians in the Old Town, living, working, trying to make their lives as tolerable as possible under the circumstances?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, I find it difficult to agree with you in relation to the 6th of December because in the morning of the 6th of December, an air-raid alarm was sounded in the morning, and there were no civilians on that morning moving about the town of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: So that would mean that the civilians were all holed up in their homes or in their businesses or in some place where they might seek shelter that your units and your battalion had led to. Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not what I'm telling you. Once an air-raid alarm is sounded, the normal thing for anyone to do is to go to a shelter to take cover. Now, whether anyone would be firing or not eventually, you don't know. However, as soon as you hear the alarm, what you do is you head for a shelter. You take cover. The air-raid alarm was sounded in the early morning hours. Therefore, people were not at work yet because it did not begin that early. They couldn't be there. The only thing they could have done is go to shelters. That sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did that come back from your intelligence that people had gone to shelters? Exactly where were the civilians over whom your position looked on that day? What did you do about the civilians in the Old Town? Tell us, please.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. We did not get any information from the intelligence officers. If there was information coming in from anyone, if there was an intelligence service manned by intelligence officers as you said, then probably they stayed elsewhere. But no such information ever reached me. I obtained my information by observing from the position of my unit, observing what I could see.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you get any intelligence that there was a mass evacuation of human beings on the 6th of December from the Old Town of Dubrovnik? Did that come back to you? Did you watch people depart from the city with your 24-hour observation?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, we did notice civilians moving about, but we didn't know what specifically they were doing. They were not jeopardising me, and therefore they were free to move about and go wherever they liked. They were not fired upon because they did not put us at risk. No one tried to prevent them from moving about any part of Dubrovnik, I'm not only talking about the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You would agree that on the 6th of December, you had -- your unit had a bird's eye, unobstructed view of the Old Town of Dubrovnik, would you not?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would agree. On the 6th of December, we could observe the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You would agree, would you not, Colonel, that attacks on civilian objects are prohibited? Would you simply agree?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there was a purely civilian target, I would agree with you. A clearly civilian target. However, if there was firing from that civilian feature --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, objection.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You didn't allow me to finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could I interrupt here and say the witness was in the middle of an answer, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: My apologies, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: He should be allowed to finish.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: My apologies. I'm sorry, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there is fire being opened from a civilian feature, a firing weapon being used to fire on military units, it ceases to be a civilian feature and becomes a military feature.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Now, would you agree, would you not, Colonel, that attacks on churches, mosques, synagogues, schools, hospitals, historic monuments, homes and palaces are prohibited, civilian all, of course? Would you not agree? They're prohibited by the law, the domestic law of Yugoslavia; they're prohibited by military regulation; they're prohibited by international humanitarian law, laws of war? You would agree with that, wouldn't you? You are a trained officer, high ranking.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to say again, Madam, if we are talking about all these buildings that you have enumerated, I fully agree. However, if from any of those buildings we noticed fire coming, it becomes a legitimate military target that can be eliminated or fired at.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Following up on something you said a few minutes ago where if civilians after the sound of an alarm or a general alert would take shelter, civilians in the Old Town would have the expectation even if a general alarm sounds of not expecting an attack on the Old Town. Would you not agree, it was after all, was it not, a UNESCO-protected territory with all its contents part of the protected area? You know that, as a trained officer of the JNA? Why should they take cover at the sound of a general alert if they're in the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they sought shelter because they also knew that there were weapons in the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: How would you be able to know what the average person knew about the status of the Old Town? I put to you that they took shelter because they knew they had been shelled before, and they feared again being shelled by those same units. That is the case, is it not, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which units had shelled. Maybe you do know, and probably that's why they were prompted to think along those lines. In any event, any normal person under war circumstances to seek shelter instead of walking around and testing his destiny and be hit.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I asked you earlier, and I don't think you were -- that you'd given an answer. Everybody in Yugoslavia from the highest officer down to the lowest officer, soldier, knows that the Old Town of Dubrovnik, certainly as of 6 December 1991 and earlier, as through the 1970s, was a UNESCO-designated World Heritage location. Isn't that a fact? And you knew it, too, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Madam, I knew that the Old Town was under UNESCO protection. I spent a lot of time in that town.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You indicated yesterday that perhaps one or maybe none of the operators of the Maljutkas had ever fired live ammunition or live projectiles prior to coming into combat. Now, on the 6th of December, persons who may never have had training on live ammunition under your command fired Maljutkas at targets, did they not?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is absolutely not true. None of the men who was not trained could have been given an order to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: A person who anyway never have fired live projectiles before was nonetheless given an opportunity or had to - because of what you deemed combat - fire. That is the case, isn't it, that not every person who fired Maljutkas had previously fired live projectiles?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, you asked me more than one question. First of all, it is impossible for such an order to be given to anyone that they had to fire from a weapon that they were not trained to do. So that's impossible. Secondly, what you say, that someone who had never fired or guided an anti-tank missile, it was possible for a person who underwent training because there's a normal training procedures applied in peacetime, and there is a shortened training period applied in wartime. So it is impossible to secure that every operator before they're sent to the front to guide a live missile, regardless of the fact that he had done that before, he did have a lot of -- he did a lot of firing during training, and he's therefore deemed to be fully trained and skillful. I still can't see anything on my screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You have no transcript?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's all right now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Good. So then if we understand each other, persons who had gone through training, although not with live projectiles, may have been firing on the 6th of December? Trained, but not having used live projectiles. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we can agree on that, that they had underwent training and that they guided missile in actual situations.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: With your recoilless guns, how many shells or how much -- yes, how many shells did your unit fire on the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My unit did not fire a single missile from recoilless guns because this weapon does not use missiles, but rather cumulative bullets.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And how much --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think there may have been some translation confusion there from the English to the B/C/S. The question wasn't dealing with missiles.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It wasn't. I think I said shells.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Pieces of ammunition, whatever correct terminology. How many, if you want to use the term bullets, did your unit fire on the 6th of December from your recoilless guns?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you the exact number because I can't remember, 10, 20, perhaps. And they were not used to fire, but rather to target, and that's the basic distinction in terminology. There's one thing when you fire for fun. And when you target, it's targeting an objective.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: How many Maljutkas targeted objects in the Old Town on the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I am told there is no audio for the colonel. You have it now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'll repeat my question. Can you hear me, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: How many Maljutkas targeted an objective in the Old Town on the 6th of December, Maljutkas in your unit?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I must clarify something. Are you referring specifically to the missiles themselves, how many of them were fired and --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, how many projectiles.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's clear. We understand each other. We engaged one target on the right-hand tower. That was an anti-aircraft gun to the right of the entrance to the old port.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: With how many projectiles?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, one projectile.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And what effect did that have? What did you know at the time? What effect did it have?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The effect was that it hit the edge of the opening from which this gun was firing, and after that this gun became silent.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Can you give us the time of day when this occurred, please.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you exactly which time of the day it was. But it was in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you not make a record or a note or communicate the fact that you had neutralised or you thought you had neutralised a target or an objective in the Old Town? Was that not worthy of recordation [sic]? Was that not an important event about which you deemed to be an enemy position?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not any kind of major event in the situation where you have operations all the time, when you're constantly being fired at. It is totally irrelevant whether this particular effect was achieved. It was indeed achieved because, as I said before, this gun stopped firing from that particular position.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Before you unleashed your Maljutkas on that gun, as you say you did, did you communicate either directly or through your chain to the other side, to the Croatians, to remove or cease from any activity with that weapon -- remove that weapon or cease any activity? Did you do that?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Madam. I did not request them to stop firing from these firing pieces, and I believe that that would be completely out of place. When you are being targeted, what are you expected to do? To wait that you get killed first and then respond? Or just stand by and silently watch what the other side is doing?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do I understand you correctly that it was not a particularly important event worthy of recordation [sic] Or notice, and yet you say that you had to be concerned about waiting to get killed first and then responding? Do you not see a bit of a contradiction in the importance that this weapon, the alleged weapon you say you saw, may have had if it was something you thought might have been killed?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, any weapon or firing piece can get you killed. But please understand that there was war, and that there was firing all around you, that all kinds of ammunition was flying around. And your primary interest and concern is to find shelter and to carry out your task to prevent firing or to eliminate the specific firing piece that was endangering you, and it is only normal that the opposite side was doing the same. Their intention was to eliminate our firing pieces in order to protect themselves from our fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In your training in the JNA, you, of course, were trained in the laws of war which would include the Geneva Conventions and the additional protocols, things that are called humanitarian law, international law. Isn't that right? You were trained as an officer and responsible for enforcing those provisions, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We studied the international laws of war at the academy, and we adhered to these conventions and laws.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you attempt to neutralise - by you, I mean you or units under your command - attempt to neutralise the mortar which you claim to have seen firing at the south tower?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never claimed that it was seemingly fired. This mortar was pointed at Srdj, and it was opening fire. From the position where I was, I could clearly see that because the mortar was laterally turned toward me, and I could clearly see it was aiming at Srdj. And we neutralised this mortar as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: How did you neutralise that mortar? With what weaponry?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was neutralised by a shell fired from a recoilless gun.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: A recoilless gun that was part of your unit on Zarkovica?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you make a note of the event and what time it occurred? Why don't you tell us what time that actually did occurred, the neutralisation of the mortar on the south tower?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The mortar on the south tower was neutralised in the early morning hours, and I repeat, there was no point or need for me to note down every single hit, every single target, every single shell. Quite simply, it was impossible under such conditions. If you believe that I was sitting there as I'm sitting now and that I was directing my units here and there, you should realise that a unit covers a wide area, and the minimum distance between two guns is 60 to 100 metres. The smallest distance between two launchers is also 60 to 100 metres. So you can see for yourself or realise how big an area a unit covers, and it is impossible for you to be at every place at every moment telling everyone what to do. If an officer, a company commander would do that, then that wouldn't be a proper army procedure. That is why we have training. That is why people are trained also to carry out tasks independently.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did someone independently give an order to neutralise those so-called targets in the Old Town? Did you give that order?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall exactly whether I issued this order to neutralise this target or if it was a platoon commander. I personally observed the target, and I noticed when the target was neutralised. I said that there was evidence, video footage made by B92 Television shot from the position where somebody was talking to a soldier who was a gunner and who, in fact, fired at this mortar.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I want to make sure I understand you correctly. You're telling this Chamber that possibly a platoon commander undertook a decision to fire a projectile into the Old Town of Dubrovnik, a UNESCO-protected site, without getting an order from a superior commander? Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I put it to you, Madam, that you are twisting the facts. We are talking about targeting a mortar, not --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I ask you to answer the question. And if I have to, I will ask His Honourable Judge Parker to assist in asking you to answer the question and not question me.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, no one could issue an order, either I or the platoon commander or anyone, to target the Old Town. That is the answer to the question that you put to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Then who issued the order to target the Old Town from Zarkovica?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one issued an order to target the Old Town from Zarkovica or was the Old Town targeted from Zarkovica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: How many projectiles did you use to neutralise the mortar?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To neutralise the mortar, one projectile was used.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And what was that?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a reactive-shaped charge.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: From which weapon?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said. From a recoilless gun.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you neutralise or fire at the persons you saw carrying crates in the Old Town or to the gates of the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Madam. These persons were fired at, these persons who were carrying ammunition from the fish shop to the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What did you fire at these persons?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, these were projectiles from a recoilless gun.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Under your -- the gun came from your unit?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, would you repeat your answer. My question was: "The gun came from your unit?" The interpreter did not hear your response.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can repeat the answer. The gun was from my unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: How many projectiles were used to neutralise the persons carrying the crate?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say with certainty, but I think it was two or three projectiles.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You cannot say with certainty, but you do have to account for your ammunition, do you not?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, it's not accounting for; it is reporting. But if you think that in combat I have time to count the ammunition that was fired, I don't have that kind of time. Neither I nor any other commander. Once combat is over, then the soldiers concerned report how much ammunition was used to their platoon commander. Platoon commanders report to me. During combat, if it is realised that two-thirds of the available ammunition are used, then I send a report to the superior command asking for reinforcement in ammunition. If there is not this kind of consumption, then it is only natural that after combat these calculations are made.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you kill the persons who were carrying the crates -- crate?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see that, and I cannot testify about anything to that effect, either yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you notice if persons were -- had fallen as a result of what you call neutralising? Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not notice that these persons fell. But they no longer returned to that feature.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And you indicated yesterday that you did not see the contents of the crate. That was your testimony yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct, I did not see the contents of the crate.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. What time of day did this occur, the neutralisation of the crate carriers?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you the exact time yet again. But it's also in the morning hours. It could have been 9.00 or 10.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What time did the -- what time do you recollect the attack on Srdj starting?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The attack on Srdj started at daybreak, if you mean to the time of day. If you meant the date, that is the 6th of December.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'd like a time, please. What time were you ordered to report so as to participate in the attack on Srdj? What time were you ordered to be up and running?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember the exact time. But it was probably around 5.00 in the morning. As I said, this is just an assumption because daybreak is at about 6.15, something like that. It is usual that a report is sent on combat readiness one hour before combat actually starts.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you demand, or you do demand, I'm sure, of the persons under your command discipline and timeliness in their responses to orders, do you not?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. That's the way it is. This is quite normal.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If you told someone under your command to report to you at 5.00 and that person didn't report at 5.00 but came in at 5.15, what would be your reaction?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd ask for the reasons why he did not report at 5.00 but at 5.15. Perhaps the person's reasons were justified; perhaps he had some business that could not be put off, and therefore he reported only then.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And you would know that the person didn't report at 5.00 but at 5.15 because you could look at a watch or clock or timepiece and know what time it was, wouldn't you? That is what normal people do, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the way it is, Madam. But it's different when we're sitting in an office, and now whether your bus was five minutes late and whether you were late on account of that, and it's a different thing when you're moving about in the dark among the rocks. You could have fallen somewhere and broken your leg in the bushes, and nobody can know what happened to you and where you are. That's a completely different situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: So you never looked at your watch once on the 6th of December 1991. Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not saying that I never looked at my watch. But had I been looking at my watch nonstop, I would not have been able to observe the battlefield and all the other activities that I was supposed to take care of on that day. If I was supposed to look at my watch all the time and to keep track of the time and minutes and whatever. Even if I had done that, believe me, my memory is not good enough to enable me to recall all of that 13 years later.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Now, you just indicated that you can't keep count of projectiles, that that is not something you would do. Perhaps you could help us understand, then, where the count in the document, the Exhibit D113, your report of 8 December, where that information comes from if you don't keep track of projectiles?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, first of all, I did not say that I did not care about how many projectiles were involved. I just said that during combat, I could not count all the projectiles. I don't think there's a single officer who could do that. Finally, once combat is over, there is a chain of command, a chain of information where reports are sent about the ammunition that was used. I've already explained that during the operations itself, I would have informed about ammunition if the ammunition level had exceeded two-thirds. But I had no need to do that. Therefore, it is only natural that after combat, I spoke to all the commanders of the subordinate units and asked them how much ammunition had been used.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: There are very specific numbers in D113. Now, keeping count -- perhaps it might help you if you took a look at D113. You have in front of you your report. And you were able in this report to be quite specific about the number of pieces that were expended both by Maljutka and by the recoilless. Now, were these kept record of during the course of combat to know that these were expended?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, of course these records were kept. We have been talking about that all the time. Look at the date when I wrote this report. This is upon completion of combat operations; that is to say, that I brought all the information together then. Now you asked me whether I was actually counting the projectiles during combat.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Does this report represent everything that you expended, all the expenditures on the 6th of December? It does, doesn't it? This is your final report, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is information about these expenditures.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Maybe -- can you tell us, please, where is the reference to the expenditure for the neutralisation of the persons carrying the crates, and where is the expenditure for the neutralisation of the mortar at the south tower? It's not there, is it, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where the N72 reactive-shaped charge is recorded, it says "fish shop near the entrance into the Old Town, four were noticed."

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What were you aiming at? You didn't indicate what you were neutralising. Sorry, I beg your pardon. The crates are there. Tell us, please, the mortar, where is it?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seems that I did not record it here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Just taking a look at that report while you have it in front of you, you said earlier that you neutralised the anti-aircraft gun with one projectile. Now, I'm looking at your own report, and it looks like -- it says "entrance of the right fortress two pieces under the recoilless, and window on the right tower, one piece." So we're not looking at one projectile, are we? We're looking at three.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: So this is not correct. If it was just one, you have put down -- this is not accurate? Which is it? Is it one or is it three?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, if you look at this, you can see that these are two different types of ammunition. We have the 9K-11 projectile which hit the window on the right-hand tower, and then, in brackets, PAT anti-aircraft gun, one piece. And then here it says about the reactive-shaped charge that hit the gate to the tower. In a military sense, this is perfectly normal. We noticed that the projectile did not directly enter the window, but rather hit the window ledge. It was perfectly normal for personnel to start retreating from that position, and we tried to prevent that. And that's why the gate to that room was targeted.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And when did you notice this?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean, when did I notice that?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: When did you notice whether or not you had hit what you thought was your target?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The impact was to the edge of the window which was targeted by the gun. And you see the moment the projectile hits the target down there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You remember we discussed the statement that you made, the interview that you gave to the officers of the OTP in Belgrade. And you were asked about various matters in the Old Town. And I will indicate, you were asked: Stepping back a bit and thinking again about the battle itself, and related to what you've put in your report, what did you fire, what did your company fire the recoilless shells at? I think you said ten recoilless shells, is what you told the OTP. It says fire the ten recoilless shells at, what did they fire. And your answer was: "First, we tried to hit this mortar right here, mortar in Stari Grad, and secondly we tried to hit this window from which this recoilless gun was active, was firing. In an indirect way, we learned about the effects. We learned about the effects of our firing at the specific mortar only 10 or 15 days ago while watching the commentary on B92 TV station. They showed this documentary on Dubrovnik, and they spoke about these issues during the show." Now, you're telling us today that you learned about the effects now, and you told the OTP then that you learned about them only some 13 years later. Now, which is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence objects to this sort of putting the evidence to the witness, what the witness allegedly said. My learned friend and colleague keeps using such terms as "I believe you said this" or "I believe you said that." Are these actually quotes? Is she quoting one of the statements, quoting one of the transcripts and putting these quotes to the witness? That's one thing. And secondly, if she wishes to cross-examine him on these points, I think he should be shown the transcripts and statements in question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm happy to do so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I don't know what time the break is. I have to find the B/C/S. But I can read --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I suggest you at least quote his words from the statement that you have. The break will be about a quarter of an hour from now. You have time to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Sure. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Nesic, I will take you back, for purposes of the English so that counsel may follow, it is 2547-1A-English, and not page 9 out of 15. So as to put it in context, the investigator starts out and asks: "And were other company commanders asked to write reports?" And your recorded answer: "Yes, company commanders from the mortar battery was asked to do this, and I suppose the battalion commander was asked to do the same, although personally I did not see him write this report or statement." Investigator: "Stepping back a bit and thinking again about the battle itself, and related to what you have put in your report, what did you fire? What did your company fire the ten recoilless gun shells at? What did they fire the ten" - and there is something inaudible - "at?" He repeats himself. Your recorded answer: "First we tried to hit this mortar right here, mortar in Stari Grad. And secondly we tried to hit this window from which this recoilless gun was active, was firing. In an indirect way, we learned about the effects. We learned about the effects of our firing at the specific mortar only 10 or 15 days ago while watching the commentary B92 TV station. They showed this documentary on Dubrovnik." And it goes on. Now, this was 2nd of September 2003. Did you learn about the effects, as you told the Chamber today, at the time or did you learn about the effects some 13 years or 12 years later?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, first of all the quote you put to me is not correct. I never spoke to you on the 2nd of September.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If my date is wrong, I will correct the date. But it was in the autumn of 2003. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I didn't catch -- I didn't get what you said before 2003, what the date was that you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I thought it was -- I'll check, but in September of 2003. Now, it was autumn of 2003, wasn't it, that we met in Belgrade? We only met one time, didn't we?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we met in the autumn of 2003. More specifically, the 25th of November.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: My apologies if I have the date taken incorrectly from documents. Now, I've read back to you your recorded answer. Can you tell us, please, when did you learn the effects of the neutralisation of these objectives? At the time of firing or in 2003 through a video made by B92?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My apologies. I have a copy of the transcript in the Serbian language, and I was not able to find the right page immediately. Madam, my transcript reads differently from what you just put to me, first of all. On that very day, after we fired, of course I observed the impact. And what it says here is in an indirect way, the firing of the mortar, about 10 or 15 days ago, was shown as part of a coverage on Dubrovnik, and the conversation was taking place in this show. And I really didn't keep that in mind while we talked there to bring these documents along and what the names were of these people. This just confirms my words, what was said in this TV programme, my words to you that there was TV footage and a documentary that was made by a TV station. That's what I said. I never said that I found out about that as I watched that particular show or programme.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You make mention of a mortar in Stari Grad. That's also in the Serbian language, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What you have testified to in this court is that there was a mortar in the south tower. You have here a mortar in Stari Grad. Which is it?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, I did tell you this back in Belgrade. Can you please show the map that I drew for you in Belgrade, the diagram, and where I marked the position of the mortar at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would like you, please, to answer my question. You said a mortar in Stari Grad. And you've talked today about a mortar in the south tower. Which is it?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The exact position of the mortar was on the south tower facing the sea, which is part of the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Is there a particular -- was there a particular problem in your head at the time we were meeting where you chose not to say the south tower. You are suddenly able to pinpoint exactly now but not then?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, I have no time to go through the entire transcript now, but I'm sure I did say back then that it was the south tower. I drew a diagram for you, some sort of a map. You should still have it from that conversation we had. And I marked accurately the position of the mortar, where it was. I marked the anti-aircraft gun, the machine-gun, as well as four other mortars that were just outside the town wall. And I signed the diagram for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And you accept that what you said at the time was mortar in Stari Grad. Correct? In this paragraph I just read to you? In Serbian, it's the same thing, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely what it says. But that was how our conversation unfolded. That's what we talked about. And we did not get tied down to that particular position. I'm sure I can find it in the transcript later on where exactly it was and where I was marking the places that Mr. Raji Murugan asked me about, asked me about personally. We confirmed those parts, and I signed the sketch that we're talking about which is in your possession.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness has referred to this sketch, and it's also referred to in the transcript of the interview that he marked out for the Prosecution accurately on the sketch the weapons that he has talked about. Can this sketch please be shown to the witness --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am sorry. I have to object --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may please finish what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We are here -- I was going to say playing with each other, but that would be putting it too low. Unless, Ms. Somers, you put to the witness the diagram, please understand that the Chamber can make nothing of the cross-examination you've made on this point. One could debate all day whether the south tower is part of the Old Town or is the wall of the Old Town and whether there's a difference.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If I could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The witness keeps making the point that he marked the position of mortar on a sketch for you. Unless and until the Chamber sees that, we have really not advanced on this point.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If you don't want to put the map or the plan to him, well, understand the Chamber can make nothing on this point.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If I may after the break resume on this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. If it's possible for me to pick up on this after the break, I would appreciate it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Colonel Nesic, we have a few minutes before we pause. You indicated that Captain Kovacevic was not moving about on Zarkovica, but he was in some sort of what you called office of yours. You were, however, were moving about, weren't you, on the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I was moving about.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And where were you moving about? What were your movements, if you can tell us, between what and what?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Madam, it's really difficult for me to specify the area because we should all be familiar with the ground there so that I could tell you between which piece of shrubbery and which tree I was moving. I was moving around Zarkovica which doesn't mean just the tower. There's a whole feature there. It's a hill and there are paths and roads passing by. I told you my position was at about seven or eight hundred metres. I had to see one unit and the other unit. I had to be able to observe the area. I had to be able to carry out all the activities which could only mean that I had to move about the area, which is precisely what I was doing. I don't know what your idea is. You can't just put a commander somewhere and then he stays put. You can't control and carry out combat operations like that with the commander put in the same spot all the time, not being able to observe what's going on around him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The -- excuse me. While you were moving around, did you make note of what munitions or projectiles were being expended as you were moving around from place to place on Zarkovica?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, I'm afraid I don't understand the question, what exactly do you mean? Which projectiles were being expended?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Were you taking -- were you paying attention to every aspect of firing that came from men under your control, your command and control, on Zarkovica that morning as the events unfolded? Plainly, did you know exactly who was firing what at what?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at every single point in time during the operations. I didn't know which specific person was firing or at what target. Whoever was near me at the time would have known, and those who were at a distance of 700 metres away from me, they would report as to what the target was of their firing, or I would just go over to them to see exactly what it had been.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is about 11.00. Would it be convenient to take a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. We will resume at 20 past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Colonel Nesic, what was the calibre of the mortar that you indicated was neutralised on the 6th of December by your units?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an 82-millimetre mortar.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I have got for the ELMO, please, the copy of the diagram, the sketch which -- I'm not necessarily planning to exhibit it, but I will pass it around. I have a copy for the ELMO, as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Colonel, while this is being passed around, the portion of your recorded statement that I am referring to, at least in the English, relates to what is labelled 2546 for counsel, side B, page 7 of 12. 2546, side B, 7 of 12. I'm not clear that your Serbian language one will be identical. In the course of the interview, a discussion came up where the investigator said: "I think the best thing is if you could just make a sketch of the Old Town. Just for the record, Colonel Nesic is drawing the sketch of the Old Town and will be putting in the positions of Croatian weapons." Your recorded answer: "I will draw our tactical sign or symbol for these special pieces of equipment." Then you say: "This is the Gradska Kafana, City Cafe. This is the entrance to Gradska Kafana from the Old Town. On the side towards the harbour there are arches. Regular machine-gun was shot from there, from this location. Towards the centre of the Old Town in direction of the seaside, there was 82-millimetre mortar. Here close to the harbour, there are a few windows, and from one of them the anti-aircraft gun was firing. As I told you, there was a show or news broadcast on TV Sarajevo which shows a specific anti-aircraft gun" - and then something is unintelligible - "and its positions." Question to you: "When were these weapons alleged to be in these positions?" Your recorded answer: "The machine-gun was there when we came to Zarkovica the first time, and this mortar and this anti-aircraft gun were used either on the 5th or 6th of December. And the 82-millimetre mortars were here on 5, 6, and 7 November, as I previously mentioned. I can't remember the date." Do you recognise the drawing, the sketch, Colonel? Is that the sketch that you made? Is it in front of you, sir? Colonel Nesic, can you hear me? I'm sorry, can you hear me, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have it in front of me. That's the sketch that we made when we had our conversation. And that's the one that I had just now referred to.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Now, would you be able to -- now, this seems to be a mixture of various dates. Is that correct? You've made reference to in your recorded answer, you talked about an 82-millimetre mortar that was on the 5th, 6th, and 7th November, but you have nonetheless shown a mortar here, albeit there may be things you say were present on the 6th of December. Is this a map that reflects a mixture of dates?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the transcript, it is clearly seen that it refers to a multitude of dates; that is, the targets in November and in December. So from the transcript, you cannot see clearly as we could at the time when we were sitting at the same table and I was pointing out to you that this and this target was in November and this and this was in December just as I did now. We discussed that, and that is what the transcript reflects as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: So that it is perhaps more clear, when you placed a mortar on this sketch, would you indicate, please -- are you able to point? Do you have a pointer, a little indicator there?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And that was the mortar you were referring to. Now --

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. That was the mortar that I referred to on the south tower facing the sea, it's semi-circular. However, at the time when we made this sketch, it was an approximate sketch of the Old Town. It did not represent all the towers, but this was this particular one, southern-most tower.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Perhaps you could help clarify, when I have just read from your recorded answer, you said, "towards the centre of the Old Town in direction of the seaside, there was an 82-millimetre mortar." Are you referring to the same weapon?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that same weapon that was on this tower. And for the sake of orientation, we said that this tower was somewhere close to the centre of the town or in respect of the rest of the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much for clarifying that. We can move away from this. Colonel, if we can move on, I want to ask you, please, the anti-aircraft weapon, the gun, the anti-aircraft gun you have referred to, how many barrels did it have?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say exactly how many barrels it had. I can only deduce that according to the flash that could have been seen from the muzzle.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Well, now, if it was a 20-millimetre gun, it would have had, would you agree, either one barrel or three barrels?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I absolutely agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Now, in neutralising it or attempting to neutralise it, you used direct-fire weapons?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: So you had to be looking at the actual weapon in order to target it, would you not?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. This weapon fired from the tower through a window. That means that I was targeting the window where from it had been firing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you know if anything else was in the tower by the window at the time? What or who or what was around it?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Madam, who would be behind a gun other than a soldier, a gun firing at you?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you know what was in the immediate area of the tower before you neutralised or attempted to neutralise the weapon?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean what was close to the tower, in front of the tower towards Zarkovica and the port itself, I did know what there was. There was sea. There were little boats. And no other individuals, if you're referring to those. There were no individuals moving around that particular area.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you, you're not able to tell us exactly what type of weapon it was by a description of the weapon, whether it was a single-barrel or a triple-barrel? Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you understood me correctly. I cannot give you a description because the fire coming from this kind of weapons can be recognised by the fire itself, by the rapidity of fire and similar things. Therefore, it allows you to deduce what kind of weapon is in question. But in this particular instance, the flash seen from the window was about 2 metres long.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Now, you would agree with me that you do not fire systems, rocket systems or weapons systems, from indoors; you have to have them protruding or have some means of protrusion from a building, firing outside the building. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must explain once again for those who haven't seen a missile before. A rocket is placed on an open area. A guiding cable is attached to it. And the operator guiding the missile is in cover. He only views as much as it is necessary to aim the periscope from it while the missile is being guided. The rocket itself is outdoor -- out of any covers, any buildings, and it is not fired from indoors.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm referring to the anti-aircraft weapon, the barrel of the weapon, you would agree, has to be at least exposed to the outside in order to successfully fire or pose any type of -- in order to successfully fire. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree. It does not have to be exposed at all. For instance, if you have a window there, you will place a gun where your microphone is. You will fire through the window without protruding the barrel through the window.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If you didn't see the barrel, how did you know it was an anti-aircraft weapon? How could you identify the weapon?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We identified it by the flash coming out the window according to the force of the impact and the velocity of fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to take a look at two photos of anti-aircraft guns, and maybe you can help us -- just explain a little bit about their descriptions. Just take a minute, please. Do you have in front of you, Colonel, two photos -- two depictions of weaponry, and then behind each there is a description about the gun. Right now on the screen, on the ELMO, is a weapon referred to as a -- would you agree it's an M-55 three-barrelled, triple-barrelled anti-aircraft gun?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would agree that this is a 20/3-millimetre anti-aircraft gun.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And then the second photograph you have is of an M-50 -- hang on a second. Is it M-57, I think? Does that sound right, a single barrel?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's a 20/1 anti-aircraft gun.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you're indicating that it was an anti-aircraft gun that was in a tower that was neutralised by your units. Now, let's just take a look for a moment if we can, let's start with the single barrel Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond one, the M-57. There is a description behind it. And this comes effectively from sources provided by the Defence. Where the weight of the weapon is shown as 300 kilograms. And it says: "Total length of firing position, 3800 millimetres." What is that in feet? I think that's around 12 feet. I'm trying to get the conversion roughly. So that would be barrel length. Would you agree that those -- you're familiar with these statistics on this type of weapon, are you not? The length of the barrel and the weight of the piece?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree. That's not the exact length of the barrel. That's the total length of a gun in a combat position.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Sorry. I have to make sure -- I think I've just lost the translation. Just one second. What would you give as a length of the barrel?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The barrel is about 2 metres long. I can't say more precisely, and that's an approximate length. 1.70 or 2 metres, because that's not a weapon that I had personal experience with.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Does this compare at all, say to an Oerlikon? Are you familiar with an Oerlikon, 20 millimetre?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, I would have to take a look at what weapon you are referring to, and then I could probably make a comparison or maybe not. I don't know what an Oerlikon is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I can ask the usher, perhaps, just to put a picture of one on the ELMO for all. I will have to share the statistics on that one. I'm told by Ms. McCreath that she has made copies of it. If I could have one, I would be grateful. Does that weapon look similar to, let's say, the single barrel that you have been looking at, at least for purposes of describing a single barrel anti-aircraft weapon?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At first glance, what I can see from this photocopy, there are similarities, and we could dispute that these are approximately identical weapons. However, there are some major differences, at least as far as the length of the barrel is concerned, especially when we talk about 20-millimetre calibre. Since the calibre is identical, it depends what kind of charge, what kind of shells are used, what the range and the power is, and all these elements have impact on the construction of the weapon in terms that a barrel may be shorter or longer. For instance, 12.7 Browning could be classified as an identical weapon to this one, however it has a different length of the barrel.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Can I just ask you, then, you mentioned the single barrel we talked about was about 1.7 or 2 metres. And the reason I'm showing you the Oerlikon is simply that it shows barrel length of 2.24 metres. So in terms of length, it's not that substantially different, would you agree? I'm only showing it because it actually shows the barrel length in its description. Would you agree that that is not that substantially different from the other single barrel? It is just help us to know if it's not too radically different.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, I've said already on the basis of what can be seen here, I cannot assist you. Basically, it does seem to be similar, but I've never actually seen one of these in real life. And I do not have exact technical and tactical information here, so I cannot really say anything. We can say that approximately it is similar, similar calibres. Now, whether the range is shorter, longer, and what kind of ammunition it uses, that is something I cannot discuss at this point in time because I have to have all this information in order to be in a position to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Now, let's look at the three-barrel weapon, the picture that you have, the M-55. And it has a picture of a man, so maybe it helps to put the scale a little bit better, little bit more helpful. Now, that barrel length -- well, that description is total weight, 1350 kilograms. Again, it uses a term, total length of firing position. But in the absence of an absolute total length of barrel, would you estimate it to be -- could you give an estimation of the length of those barrels, please?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The total length of barrels is the same as in the case of a 20/1-millimetre cannon because practically this artillery piece, three 20/1-millimetre weapons were put together. Here they are all together. The gun cannon that we are looking at now is quite different from a 20/1-millimetre weapon that we looked at a few minutes ago. It is operated manually. It has three barrels, and it has an engine. It uses gasoline as a fuel. So it moves the barrels up and down and in circles, whereas in the 20/1-millimetre gun, this is all done manually. We can see here also the wheels of this particular artillery piece. Also, for the 20/1-millimetre weapon, we see that it goes down, the bipod, and then it is easier for it to move about, whereas in the case of a 20/1-millimetre gun, these wheels part, and then it is put on a tripod as we saw a few minutes ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Now, if as we understand it you say that a weapon, and you've not been able to tell us whether it was a single-barrel or a triple-barrel or what number of barrels, but if in fact there was an anti-aircraft weapon, gun, in a tower, the barrel would logically would be protruding, would it not? Some portion of that barrel would be protruding, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, it is not logical for it to be protruding. That would be the case if this were a very small room, 3 by 3 metres, for example. However, if you have a tower that is much bigger, there is no need for the barrel to be protruding.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The weight of these weapons to be taken up to those towers would pose or would require considerable effort. You would agree with that, wouldn't you? These are old towers, are they not? This is not contemporary architecture; this is historic old tower we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, no effort is required to have this done. To bring the weapon in requires only two men, although that is the weight that was mentioned. The weapon was constructed in such a way that once it is lifted, it is placed on wheels at its bipod, and then one man can manipulate it on his own, pull it back or forth, wherever, position it wherever without feeling any kind of great weight in his arms. You have realised that this involves the physics, that it was the centre of gravity that was used for manipulating this weapon.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You would agree that it would take some effort to get a weapon that weighed 1350 kilograms up to a tower or a weapon that weighed 300 kilograms up to a tower. It is not simply a 1, 2, 3 affair?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, I cannot agree with you. I told you already that I was in Dubrovnik many times and that I know the tower very well and all other features in this town. There is an entrance, a big door on the side. So there is no need for you to have this lifted manually or in some other way. There is a system, of course, for bringing the weapon to that position. Secondly, even if they were operating from there at the time, that means that preparations were carried out beforehand, or rather that a platform was made from which the gun could be operated. I did a similar thing in Zarkovica where I prepared a platform and lifted the weapon about 2 metres so that I could fire above the wall. A recoilless gun is also very heavy if you want to lift it only physically. However, if you handle it properly, there is practically no physical strain involved on the part of the manpower handling the weapon.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You have indicated that you have had continuous observation of this area, of all that was in view of Zarkovica, which would include this area, since your units were on Zarkovica. And are you suggesting that it would be a matter of no effort at all for someone within the Old Town to elude, to escape your view and carry or ferry up to a tower, an old tower, a weapon weighing some 300 or perhaps 1350 kilograms and simply not be seen? Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, if you wish, I can put it to you that way, and I can explain it to you in the following way: Not a single soldier, not a single person in a theatre of war --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may the witness please finish answering. He was cut in mid-sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not a single soldier in a theatre of war would not be crazy enough to be doing something in broad daylight when they can be seen by anybody. So of course they do it during night, moving a weapon from one place to another and so on and so forth. And especially since this is a tower, who can see through the walls what is going on inside?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Not even you could see through the walls what was going on inside. Your units had no idea what was going on inside, did they? You did not even know if there, in fact, was a fire, or any kind of firing coming from that weapon, did you? In fact, there was no weapon, was there?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, there was a weapon, and the weapon was firing. And that can be seen clearly, that the weapon was firing. That cannot be concealed, the firing of such a weapon. There is not a silencer or any such thing for this kind of weapon. Every shot is readily discernible through the flames, the flares. Also, if you look at this part here and if you can see the flames and flares coming through all these holes, not only through the muzzle. And this creates this big spectrum around the gun. If you would see this gun firing at nighttime, you would see it as if it were in broad daylight because it lights up an area of 50 to 100 metres all around it because the flare coming from the weapon itself is so strong.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Colonel, it is a fact, is it not, that a barrel length that is at least, let's say, 1.7 to 2 metres and possibly in excess, if it is visible to your units, it is going to be visible to everyone else monitoring activity in the Dubrovnik area including the European Community monitors, including other internationals; it is not something that would simply escape observation. You surely could not be the only persons taking note of such a weapon, could you?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not the only person from my unit. There must have been at least 10 or 15 other persons who noticed this gun firing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Because the barrel would have had to protrude, Colonel, and you are the only persons who noticed it among hundreds of other persons, or dozens of other persons rather, who may have been tasked with observing the status of the Old Town. Isn't that right, only you noticed it?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Madam. But I don't understand your question at all. I did not hear the beginning of the interpretation. Could you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Certainly. Colonel, it is a fact, is it not, that a barrel that is at least, let's say, 1.7 to 2 metres and possibly in excess, if it is visible to your units, it is going to be visible to everyone else monitoring activity in the Dubrovnik area, including the European Community monitors, the ECMMs, the men in white, including other internationals? It is not something that would escape observation or notice. You surely could not be the only persons taking note of such a weapon, could you? That was my question.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, you are talking about the barrel, and I told you that we did not see the barrel. We saw the flare coming from the window. It is correct that someone else could have seen it, too, if they were in that kind of position, if they could see the place where this came from. You cannot expect someone from Lapad to see a gun firing from the Old Town when there is no view of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In your version of it, there is no record at all of the existence of this weapon, is there? There is no official record even on the part of the JNA, is there, Colonel? Is there?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for whether there are any official notes on the existence of such a weapon or not is something that I cannot discuss now because I don't know who has information and of what nature. I am talking about what I saw from my position and about what specifically happened on that day. Now, whether somebody recorded that, in which way, which side is something I cannot discuss, Madam. I cannot talk about that, whether somebody does or does not have information.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'd like to ask the usher, please, to show D62 and D65.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Colonel, when did you first note this anti-aircraft gun?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The moment when it started firing, that moment. Before that, we did not know that it was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What date was that? Sorry, before I distract you with any documents, what date was that? When did you first notice the existence of this weapon?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically on the 6th of December 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And so intelligence would have indicated or passed up the existence of this weapon on that date, would it not, Colonel? Colonel, before you continue reading, can you hear me? There would have been reports --

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
