utterances.text: I've heard your question. Whether it would be sent further up or not, that is something that I'm not going into. I wouldn't go into that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If you were concerned about its possible effect on your units, then it would also possibly affect other units. Would you agree? It isn't something that could be held close to your chest. You had to make sure that its existence was well-enough known for the safety of your own units. Wouldn't you agree?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not right, Madam. The position that this weapon was at made it possible only to -- for it to fire at my unit, not any other unit from that battalion. It could only fire at me or at sea. It could not fire at any other unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: By your own indication, it was no big deal to get it up or down. It could have been moved and posed a threat. Couldn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you would carry it out of that tower, if you could take it to some other position, then it could pose a threat to someone else. But I'm saying that from that position that it was firing from at that time, it could only fire at me or at the sea. That was the area that it could engage.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Please take a look at D62. It's a report of 6 December at 1700 hours. Can you tell us, please, where there is a reference to this anti-aircraft weapon in this document? This is the report of the combat activities, the 6th of December 1991. Please find reference to the anti-aircraft weapon.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't found any reference here to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: That's because it's not there, is it?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's not mentioned in this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if you would take a look, please, at D62 -- 65. I'm so sorry, Colonel. That is a report to the first administration. Do you know who General Simonovic is, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Simonovic? No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Now, this is a report that was sent by the commander of the 9th Naval Sector. And I'd like to ask you, please, if you could find in this report, which details the action on Srdj, if you can please find the reference to weapons being found in the Old Town of Dubrovnik, where it specifically mentions "the Old Town of Dubrovnik." Or of an anti-aircraft weapon in the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I've found no reference to such a weapon in the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Yesterday, and we will move on in the interests of time. We have to pick up our pace a bit. Yesterday, you spoke of an area called Lovrinac. I hope I'm pronouncing it correctly. Lovrinac. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. And you mentioned a tunnel and a park in connection with Lovrinac. Now, that park is - I hope I'm pronouncing it right - Gradac park. That's the park, isn't it? You know Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but whether the name of that park is Gradac, I can't quite remember what the name of the park was. I know there is a park there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The artillery that you claim to have seen there, you're referring to was an anti-aircraft? Are you able to tell us exactly what you saw? That was an anti-aircraft gun, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, that was no anti-aircraft gun; it works quite differently. This was an artillery piece with a strong shot, and it fires shells. And this has nothing to do with anti-aircraft guns where you have the 20-millimetre calibre, and on the other hand you have artillery pieces with a much higher calibre. I can't quite say which calibre. But from 56 millimetre onwards.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Now, the mortars near the Libertas, you did not actually see them, did you, that you referred to?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did see them, and they were observed accurately. And those were the mortars that I mentioned to you back in Belgrade. And it was on account of those mortars where the 130-millimetre support battery did not provide the support it was supposed to from Cilipi. That was the reason we had to withdraw from our positions at Srdj and return to our initial positions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: This Trial Chamber has heard evidence of a rocket launcher in that location, not mortars. Are you standing by your view that there were mortars?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is still my position that they were mortars. Perhaps there was a rocket launcher positioned there, too. It's just that I didn't notice it. But mortar activity was observed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: But you were observing the whole area, and you didn't notice something. That's what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, if that piece was not firing at me, how could I have been able to notice it? I was only in a position to notice those that were firing, those that were making their presence known. If something is concealed and is not firing at me, of course I won't notice it. I couldn't be expected to watch every single part of town at every single point in time. I would have been some sort of a supernatural officer if I'd been able to do that. If you are observing, you observe sector by sector, area by area.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Colonel, you made a reference to Charlie yesterday, and you said it was going to and from the main road. Now, that was in full view of Zarkovica and Strincijera. Correct? We agree on that?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could not see the Flying Charlie at all from Strincijera. You couldn't observe it from there. Strincijera is in quite a different place in relation to Zarkovica. As for the lower road, I didn't say the main road, the lower road when they were there, we used to call it the lower road, and the upper road was the main road itself, and the lower road was the one running parallel and leading into town, the centre down there to the Old Town and the exit from the Old Town. And it is my position that it was on the lower road that I noticed the mortar moving back and forth. It was moving from the junction or the underpass near the intersection of the roads because that's the point that I could see from up there. And all the way as far as the Old Town, and then the road is lost amid houses, and then near the harbour closer to us again you can see the road, and you can see where it goes. And you can observe that section of the road again.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I believe what you've just described contradicts what you have described and what you described and drawn yesterday. I just need a moment to take a look at it, but it is not familiar, what you just said. You had drawn yesterday -- let me ask you, please, if you can take D -- what is the number of this map? D111. Is it placeable [sic] on the ELMO, please. I'm looking at D111, and your arrow shows the vehicle going west to east, does it not?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, we can say that my arrow is showing that it was also driving from east to west because you have the arrow going in both directions. So this was the line of movement on that vehicle driving along the road that I noticed it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: That's fine --

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's marked in the middle, and then from here on --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Now -- thank you for clarifying that. If there had been, as you claim, fire, the vehicle would have stopped. Correct? Do you agree the vehicle would have stopped to fire and then moved on?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Now, in those moments, if I've understood you correctly, when it stopped, your units could have attempted to neutralise that weapon. Did you do so?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Madam. We didn't do that. And I never said anything about firing at it. In this area that we are talking about now, there was nothing said about that. Of course, he wouldn't have been crazy either to stop dead in mid-road and open fire from right there. But rather, he would try to take shelter by the side of the road if there was any shelter to be had and try firing from there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your unit was not the only unit firing at the Old Town. There were other units of your battalion also involved. Those would be, and please tell me if you agree, the 120-millimetre mortar battalion, and other -- and the 82-millimetre mortars. It was not just your units that were involved in this action. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I must point this out: I did not open fire on the Old Town, nor did my unit. Now, as to whether anyone did and which unit it was, I can't testify about that because I simply don't know which units those were.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You indicated that you were asked or ordered to give a statement about the activities and the I believe it was targets in the Old Town -- I'm sorry, targets generally that were affected on the 6th of December. How did you feel about having to do that? Had that ever been ordered of you before, to come in and describe or justify your actions?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in that sort of way, and I felt very uncomfortable because I had to do it on that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Now, did you -- I'm sorry. After you submitted this report, were you investigated further by any organs of the JNA? Were you investigated or questioned further by the members of the 2nd Operational -- by the command of the 2nd Operational Group?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, I am not aware that there was any investigation related to me, or at least no one ever told me that there was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you know Zoran Lemal? I believe you've spoken of him before.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Would you describe yourself as a friend or a colleague of Zoran Lemal?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't say, but what I can say is both.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: That you are a friend and a colleague?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Formally, in a formal sense, we were colleagues, and we were friends in our spare time. Outside working hours, we were not exactly on visiting terms, but yes, we were friends.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you consider him or do you consider him to be a good officer?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have no reason to believe that he was a good officer or a bad officer. This is something that only his superior officer can speak about. We work in two different garrisons. The distance between these two is about 300 kilometres. Therefore, I really can't pass opinion on whether he was a good officer or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In your dealings with him, have you known him vis-a-vis yourself to be truthful, honest, decent towards you?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, we had a normal relationship, exactly the kind of relationship that we should have had.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Now, he also was involved in the action on the 6th of December, was he not? He and his units.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, he was involved from Strincijera towards Srdj.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Now, at a meeting of the command or at the -- either the headquarters of the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Brigade in Brgat held after the 6th December to analyse the attack of that day, how did you react to the criticism of Zoran Lemal -- I'm sorry, the criticism, I beg your pardon, directed at you by Captain Kovacevic, Vladimir Kovacevic, concerning the fact that you overused your artillery causing too much damage to the Old Town? What was your reaction to that?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, first of all, I don't remember that I was ever criticised like that. Secondly, I had no artillery pieces, nor would I have been in a position to use any.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Criticised that weaponry was overused, causing too much damage to the Old Town. How did you feel about that, or you don't remember that?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Firstly, I told you I don't remember. Secondly, I would like to see what precisely this damage was that could be contributed to my unit's damage to stone. The anti-armour pieces could hurt steel. That was the best effect. This anti-armour rocket could pierce through 700 millimetres of pure steel, but it is also true that if you look at stone, you'll recognise the point of impact because there will be slight damage to this stone. Now, this is very hard to say having in mind the weapons I had, how they could have caused much damage to Dubrovnik. Same thing with the projectile that is fired from a recoilless gun. They have their maximum effect on steel. But if you're expecting to find a hole there in this plate of steel that has been pierced through, you won't, because the hole you will find will only have a diameter that is approximately as wide across in terms of centimetres as a cigarette.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: How did you feel about being criticised by your battalion commander for excessive activity toward the Old Town at the meeting at the battalion headquarters?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, this is the first I hear of any such criticism.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Zoran Lemal testified before this very same Trial Chamber and under affirmation, transcript page 7419, 7th of July, said the following: Question, this is about Captain Kovacevic: "Well, he told me on that same day, the 6th of December in the afternoon when he came to see me, and when I asked him `what's all this, why weren't we given fire support,' and he said he didn't know and that was the reason for everything that followed." That was his answer. Question: "Did you also in speaking with Captain Kovacevic that evening or perhaps the next day thereafter, did you tell him -- did you hear him telling Captain Nesic that, that is, the commander of the anti-armour company, that he all used his artillery over" - I'm sorry, I'm reading the transcript - "which resulted in too much of the damage to the town that Captain Kovacevic was concerned they might be held accountable. Did you hear Captain Kovacevic say anything to that affect?" Answer: "No, I did not. I did not hear anything like that." Excuse me a second. Going on to page 7419: "At this meeting, did you hear Captain Kovacevic blame Captain Nesic for all using his artillery," again it says all, I believe it's just an error in the transcript, "which caused too much damage to the town for which he expressed his concern that they would be held accountable?" Answer of Lemal: "They were some words, but I really can't remember now because I was focussed on my unit. However, there were some words of criticism addressed at Nesic but what he was criticised for specifically I don't know. But he was the person most criticised." Question: "And criticised by Captain Kovacevic?" Answer: "Yes." Question -- yeah, I'm sorry. That's all that's relevant. How did you feel about that?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already told you, Madam, this is the first I hear of it. I can't remember that I was ever criticised. Kovacevic certainly didn't criticise me. Now, as for Lemal's testimony, what he claims is: "Yes, I think there was some."

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Were you ever charged criminally for your intentional shelling of the Old Town of Dubrovnik on 6th of December 1991 by any Tribunal in the former Yugoslavia or in the current Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No charges have been filed against me because there was no reason for that because I never fired at the Old Town or inflicted any damage on that. I already explained that the weapons that I had at my disposal were not able to cause any major damage.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'll just wind up.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If the Chamber would allow me just a couple minutes to run some video footage by this witness that relates to the damage inflicted on the Old Town of the 6th, I'd be grateful. I realise it has been long, and I'm sorry, but we needed to get these points across.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. May I please ask... It will be from P66, 31.42 to 31.48.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The depiction of these -- the capturing of these vessels in the harbour by Maljutkas does not appear in the report that you gave. Oversight?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on what do you claim that these vessels were hit by Maljutka? It's not visible from that footage. One can see on the video that these two boats were on fire. Had they been hit by Maljutka, probably at least one of them would have been punctured and sunk. That's what I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Let me replay it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Even here, you can see that something explosive is coming from this ship and that it has burst into the air from the ship, so I think that there was some explosives on that boat.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you forget to include these two boats in your report, Colonel Nesic?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why you think I forgot or why should I have included them in my report, what the reason would be for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours, for the extra time. No further cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Somers. Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nesic, while you have this D11 map in front of you, I would kindly ask you to use the pointer and show us the position, again your position at Zarkovica.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could you please show us now the Strincijera position where Lemal's company was deployed.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: With respect to these two positions, you have marked the position where you noticed the movement of a Flying Charlie. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: From the Zarkovica position, did you have an unobstructed view over the zones that you have just marked where you saw this movement?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was able to see the sector except where this curve on the road was and the view was obstructed by some houses. However, as it proceeds, I could see the next section of the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, from Strincijera, was it possible to see the route of the movement of the Flying Charlie?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was impossible to see any of that sort from Strincijera.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you explain why?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can, because Strincijera, look how far back it is, how high it is above the sea level. It's 482 metres. So the only view that you have would be somewhere here at sea, and it was impossible to see the town itself at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was that due to the configuration of the terrain?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because of the configuration of the terrain, this vision was blocked, because you see this is a descending ground, steep to the coast because you see that these contours are close to one another which indicates that the closer to one another they are, that indicates a very sharp descent towards the sea. Therefore, no optical visibility was possible from this place on this place.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nesic, if you can please just slow down to allow the interpreters to translate whatever you say and that we have it on the transcript. Could you just please move the map a little so that we can see Lapad and Babin Kuk. All right. We have it zoomed on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Were you at Strincijera?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you show us with the pointer what one could see from Strincijera.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately this area towards the sea can be seen from Strincijera, including this section as well towards the sea. This area towards Mokosica.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So you were showing Babin Kuk and Lapad.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Lazaret, as it is written on the map, so this area here.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is it possible to view from Strincijera the roads on Lapad and Babin Kuk?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Partially, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When we -- when you responded to the questions asked by my learned colleague concerning anti-aircraft guns, you were shown three photographs, one Oerlikon, then a single-barrel 20-millimetre gun, and an anti-aircraft -- an M-57 anti-aircraft gun, and also a three-barrel M-55 anti-aircraft gun, all of these guns are of 20-millimetre calibre. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Are these guns of different weight?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course they are. These guns have different weights.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you have these pictures in front of you?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown the photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nesic, do these three anti-aircraft guns have identical construction or structure?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can these pieces be disassembled or are they always in the shape as we have seen them on the photographs?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As they're shown in the photographs, both these firing pieces, as I said, this one I'm not familiar with, but it's similar to the other two, are in a combat position, placed in a combat position. And this 20/1 and the Oerlikon and the 20/3 millimetres are all placed in a combat position. In these two photographs of Oerlikon and of 20/1 gun, for the 20 /1 one, there's a missing piece which is lowered. As for Oerlikon, I'm not sure whether it has it, but according to the structure, based on the structure and the similarities with our gun, I suppose that it has a certain understructure in order to transport it from one place to another.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nesic, I would again kindly ask you to speak more slowly in order for us to have everything you say on the transcript. When you explained what was missing on these anti-aircraft guns, single-barrel guns, you said several times, the term "Podvozak" [phoen] in B/C/S. Could you please explain in layman terms what you were referring to.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will show it on the ELMO, on the gun 20/3. These are, in fact, wheels, only they are attached here with the bipod, and you can see they can be elevated off the ground so that the gun does not lean on them. By contrast, the 20/1 gun has removable wheels, and it can lean on these so-called paws.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: If we compare the structures of the wheels and this transferrable part with wheels, in terms of weight and structure, is it identical in a one-barrel gun or a three-barrel gun?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not identical because the difference is, first of all, this one is composed of three pieces, so the structure is completely different. And it dictates that this be positioned and shaped in a different way. There's also a possibility that this -- that the wheels can be removed from this 20/3 gun and that it leans on its paws. So far, the other possibility is just to lift the wheels off the ground which favourably affects the rapidity, and it depends on the rapidity of air force. There are norms of changing firing position. Taking fire positions are changeable because they simply have to be able to do that in view of the velocity of operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, please, can these firing pieces be disassembled?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they can.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can they be transported in such a disassembled form?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they can. They can be transported on a vehicle or carried manually on backpack, animals or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me approximately how long it takes for this single-barrel gun to be disassembled and then reassembled again? Don't go into any details; I'm just referring to disassembling it into its major parts.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot really tell you exactly because these were anti-aircraft guns. I didn't have much experience with them. I know basically how they operate and things like that. But I cannot tell you details like that because I was more involved with infantry weapons than with these kind of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown the Defence Exhibit D35.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nesic, this is the photograph which was taken from --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have to object. This was not part of -- this particular photograph was not part of my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What is the relevance for re-examination, Mr. Rodic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is in relation with the questions asked by my learned colleague about the size of an anti-aircraft gun, about the possibility for transporting these kind of guns. The witness mentioned that it was possible to be disassembled and transported and reassembled again. That was my point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Carry on, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nesic, this photograph was taken from the P66 video presented by the Prosecution, and parts of it you could see relating to Dubrovnik. Can you tell me, please, is it possible to recognise, or rather, compare this gun that you see in this photograph with the one on D35, whether this on D35 photograph is identical to a three-barrel gun showed to you by my learned colleague? Are we talking here about identical models of weaponry? Can you make that statement?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The photograph is not very clear. But I can see that it is the same weapon, only it was shot from a different angle.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you see the position where this anti-aircraft gun is?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot determine the exact location.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: No, no, I did not ask you about the location, not position in that sense. But can you see where it is, on what?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is on the trailer of some vehicle, a tractor or a truck. I cannot say. But at any rate, it is obvious that it's on the trailer of a motor vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't need this document any longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nesic, tell me, please, your unit is an anti-armour company. You explained that you have platoons within the company. Recoilless guns, rockets, PLK911. And you explained to us what the crews of these squads and platoons are like. Can you tell us briefly in terms of establishment how many squads and platoons this would involve within your company.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within my company, there were two platoons. One platoon was that of the recoilless guns, and the other one was of anti-aircraft, guided missiles, and 9K-11. It had three squads, while the anti-armour company had six squads. And to be more precise, every squad of the recoilless guns had two recoilless guns respectively. And every squad -- every missile squad had one control panel. So that is the level of squad, that unit level.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, if these platoons and squads are deployed at positions, how many personnel are involved in observation as far as these particular weapons are concerned?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Observation is practically carried out by each and every soldier in combat. That is to say that every person that is on a position observes. In addition to observing, observation is divided within the zone of operation of that particular artillery piece. So the manpower manning one particular piece observes that area, and in addition to all of that there is a soldier who is given the role of observer, to specifically observe a particular zone. So this observer exists in a platoon, in a company, and further on depending on the unit that is engaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: If you say that every soldier observes and has that task in practical terms, does a soldier report to someone about a noticed objective?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A soldier does first report to his squad leader because that is his immediate superior who must be near him, 30 or 50 metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown D62.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nesic, you've already seen this document. My learned friend showed it to you. This is a regular combat report of the command of the 9th Military Naval Sector dated the 6th of December 1991. Could you please look at paragraph 1, "The enemy." Is there any reference to the Old Town there?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the end of paragraph 1 in the last passage, it says that "fire was occasionally opened from the Stradun region as well as from the old city port."

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Stradun and the old city port, where are they?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stradun is in the centre of the Old Town, and the Old Town port is outside the old walls.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown the sketch. Could it please be placed on the ELMO, the sketch that he made for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nesic, let us clarify this a bit, what this is all about. Can you tell us, on this sketch, there is a date, the 25th of November 2003. Is that right? Can you see it in the upper right-hand corner?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the 25th of November 2003.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is that the time when you spoke to the representatives of the OTP in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I spoke to them at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, in the left upper corner, it says "Jovica Nesic."

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Whose handwriting is that?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I think it could be the handwriting of Mr. Raji Murugan.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, in this area where the symbols are described in a text, whose handwriting is that?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is again the handwriting of Mr. Raji Murugan because I gave these explanations to him and he's the one who compiled the legend.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Please look at the words "Pile," "Zarkovica," and the word "sea" which is above the sign for mortar.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who wrote that?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know exactly. I cannot say with any certainty whether it was also Mr. Murugan or perhaps it was Mr. Philipps.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, who drew this sketch of the Old Town, the way it is drawn here?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was drawn by Mr. Raji Murugan.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you draw anything on this sketch?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Please use the pointer and indicate everything that you inscribed and tell us what it represents.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I put this sign for a machine-gun here. Then also I put this sign for a mortar here, at this tower. Then I marked this window here and I drew these three windows on this tower that exist there, and I marked the window from where the anti-aircraft gun was firing. And I marked these four mortars along the walls of the Old Town facing the Pile gate. And I initialled the sketch.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When you drew this sign of the submachine-gun, what did you tell the members of the OTP? Where was it?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Underneath the arch that the City Cafe is here, and then facing the sea there are arches and that it was underneath the arch and that is why this line was drawn this way so that this could be shown, this arch.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. I want to ask the Chamber to have counsel clarify and repeat that this diagram did not reflect simply the 6th of December, that it is a mixture. And if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It doesn't need to be repeated. That's clear in the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I meant to specify the time again, but that's not a problem. I'll be brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nesic, this submachine-gun, you explained its location now, and that's what you told the members of the Office of the Prosecution. What did you tell them? When did you see this weapon?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This weapon was seen in November when we came to the Zarkovica position.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: All right. Did you show them something else on this sketch that had to do with the month of November 1991?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These four mortars by the old city walls on the Pile side. Those that are depicted here. Later on, we agreed, Mr. Murugan said, "Can we show them with an X?" It's easier to depict them that way in the legend, it's easier than if we use the real tactical sign for a mortar.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, do you remember what the representatives of the OTP asked you in relation to these four mortars?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely, they asked me whether I saw them personally, and I said that I personally did not see them, that they are at a position from where I could not observe them or see them myself. However, that we did receive specific information two or three days later because TV Sarajevo on its evening news programme broadcast a report from there showing these four mortars and also the crews could be shown placing the shells inside and then seeking shelter running towards the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So as far as December 1991 is concerned, did you put the marks for the weapons that you noticed?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What is left over is the mortar on this tower. Can you tell us whether you described the location where this mortar was to the OTP?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did. And that is recorded in the transcript, that this is the southern-most tower facing the sea, semi-circular, and that's where the mortar was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: As for this anti-aircraft gun, did you describe where it was?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. And when we drew this sketch, I added these three windows, and I marked the middle window from where the anti-aircraft gun was firing at us.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown Exhibit P17 just for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nesic, you do recognise the photograph?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could the harbour of the Old Town be zoomed in, please. Could it be enlarged, if possible. Thank you. Mr. Nesic, since you showed windows, you depicted windows in the sketch where you saw the anti-aircraft gun, can you show us on this picture which windows these are and where the gun was.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can show that. It is in this part here. And three windows can be seen quite clearly on this tower.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you take a pencil, and can you just touch the window without making a mark.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is that the window?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is the third window -- or rather the middle window from where the weapon fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may the record reflect that on photograph P17, the witness indicated the middle window on the tower of the fort in the old city harbour. That is the location, the old city harbour. And he indicated that that is where the anti-aircraft gun was. Thank you. I won't be needing that exhibit any longer. Your Honour, I would now ask for this sketch that the witness explained in detail be assigned a number as a Defence exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The exhibit will be D114.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nesic, on several different occasions, your answers provided to the OTP were, "I did not shell the Old Town." Is that true?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is absolutely true.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you then please tell us, you or rather your unit, what did you do on the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what you mean by what we were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you in relation to the firing carried out by a unit.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We fired on such targets as had been observed, the targets that were emerging in the Old Town area as well as the broader surrounding the Old Town. And those parks, I'm not sure if I can refer to that as a broader area, so the broader area surrounding the Old Town walls.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did anyone from your unit at any point in time fire randomly at the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was no random firing. That was not possible. It's not like they were firing a rifle so you had taken shelter and now you were shooting this way and that, however you please. That's not how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nesic. Finally, do you know whether any investigation was carried out against anyone who had forbidden the use of 130-millimetre guns as support for your unit --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: -- while you were attacking the Srdj feature?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: There's no indication, first of all, to which persons, and it is certainly a question that was not raised in cross-examination. But that this witness would be able to speculate about whom the question is asked is simply not realistic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think there's some difficulty about seeing this as arising in re-examination, Mr. Rodic, forbidding the use of 130-millimetre guns.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do accept this, Your Honour. And I withdraw the question. I hereby conclude my additional examination, redirect, of Mr. Nesic. Thank you, Mr. Nesic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, before proceeding, I wanted to ask of the Court, and I apologise, I had intended to tender into evidence the photographs of the anti-aircraft weapons. And I'm sorry it wasn't done earlier because it might have made it easier for Mr. Nesic to refer to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The photograph and the specifications of the M-75, 20/1 gun will be received as one exhibit, Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P220.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And the photograph and the specifications of the M-55, 20/3 gun will be received as a Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P221.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I have not gone to the Oerlikon as that was not a weapon with which the witness was familiar, and it seems to have no place in the proceedings. Mr. Nesic, thank you very much. That concludes your evidence, and you will be pleased to know you're now free to go back to your home and your work. So thank you for your assistance. We will now adjourn and resume at 10 minutes past 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.09 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could I ask you to take the card that is given to you now and to read the affirmation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir. For the record, can you please state your full name.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: My name is Janko Vilicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vilicic, can you tell us with your educational background.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: First, elementary school, then secondary school. I obtained a degree at the engineering school in Belgrade. I obtained my Ph.D. at the Ecole National Superieur in Paris, and I pursued my further studies at the military academy in Zagreb. I have a Ph.D. in military science.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vilicic, I must ask you to speak a little slower so that everything you say may be reflected in the transcript. Since a lot of what you just stated about your educational background has not been reflected in the transcript, however, I will go through your biography in writing and the Chamber will see what it is. You have told us you obtained a Ph.D. Can you say when and on what subject?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: That was in 1986 at the military engineering academy. The subject was to do with ballistics, and I am a doctor of military engineering.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Where did you work? Where did you spend your career? Which organisation did you work for?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: After graduating from the military engineering faculty, I was an officer, and I became an active officer. I was on duty at the military technical institute of the land forces in the ballistics section. I was chief of the ballistics section. I became one in 1977, and I stayed in that position until 1985. From 1985 on, I was the chief of the information and computing centre. It was an IT centre that processed all the research, including firing tables. Since 1990, I was the assistant of the director for development of land forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vilicic, did you take part in teaching at any high schools or institutes as a civilian and as a military person?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: Yes, at the military engineering in Belgrade, also at the military engineering faculty in Sarajevo, I taught.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't get the location.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Paris at the Ecole National des Ingenieurs et Techniciens in Algeria. Also I taught in the Zagreb graduate studies for those taking an MA degree. I mentored a number of different theses, and I was also a member of the doctoral commission at the engineering faculty in Belgrade and in Zagreb. I was also a member of the scientific committee of the military technical institute and of the scientific commission of the institute for strategic investigations and research of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us when you pursued any specialised courses abroad.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: Yes, as I said, in 1964 and 55, I studied at the high military school in France at the Ecole National Normal Superieur in Paris, which I completed in 1965 and which was recognised as a specialised course.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers kindly pause between question and answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you publish any scientific works, journals or textbooks in the fields in which you were active?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was a condition for me to pursue my Ph.D. I published a number of different scientific papers. I also wrote a book which was written while I taught at the military land forces academy in Belgrade. I wrote a book called "Ballistics", and this is also a subject that I taught to the cadets of the Belgrade military academy in 1975 -- between 1975 and 1979 rather.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in addition to the expert opinion that has been filed, the biography has not been -- the CV has not been enclosed. Therefore, can we have it distributed to the Honourable Trial Chamber and my learned friends and colleagues so that you may have a written form of everything the witness has now spoken about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That could well have helped the interpreters had they had it before you went through that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, indeed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vilicic, can you please confirm this: The document that you have now been shown by the usher, is this your CV, the CV that we have tried to go through for the benefit of the Honourable Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: Yes, but there's more information here than I just stated orally.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Vilicic, pursuant to a request made to you by the Defence of General Pavle Strugar, did you draft an expert opinion? If so, please tell us what sort of expert opinion you wrote.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: It's called expert analysis of the shelling of Dubrovnik Old Town. This is an expert analysis that we wrote in both Serbian and English with annexes containing calculations, graphs, everything that went into the making of this expert's analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you have that expert analysis in front of you?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: Yes, in both Croatian and English. May I just be allowed to add something in relation to this expert opinion: We wrote this expert analysis on the basis of the documents that we have given.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vilicic, can you please follow my questions and answer my questions.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note: Can counsel please speak into the microphone, and can we please pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the interpreters please ask both speakers to speak slower for the accuracy of the transcript. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You heard those things, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vilicic, can you say which documents and which sources you used when you wrote your expert opinion?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: The basic documents we used were documents that we obtained from the Defence team, or rather that the Tribunal forwarded to the Defence team. The fundamental document is General Nojko Marinovic's testimony in writing as given to the investigators of the ICTY in the year 2000 and the transcript from General Marinovic's testimony in the Milosevic case, the testimony was to the same issues. And both testimonies were identical in substance. We used these testimonies as corroboration that the information on the special deployment of the Croatian forces was authentic. We also used Zeljko Soldo's statement which he also gave to the ICTY. We also heard some witnesses and the last one was OTP witness Ivan Negodic. That's where we decided to stop and that's where our analysis stops, with the testimony of Ivan Negodic. The next thing we used was the statement made by Admiral Jokic while he testified before the Tribunal, as well as some other witnesses whose testimonies we listened to. For example, the particular part of Djelo Jusic's testimony where he spoke about the meteorological conditions in Dubrovnik on the 6th of December. Or Ivan Grbic who spoke about the destruction of some features in Dubrovnik and some of the features that were hit. We regularly followed the progress of this case over the internet.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vilicic, according to the information that you had when you completed your expert analysis, can you tell us what the deployment was of the firing positions and units of the JNA in the Dubrovnik theatre of war.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: As for the deployment of units around Dubrovnik --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Our sound system is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There appears to be a problem with the sound system, if you could pause for a moment, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could the witness say something to see if we can hear something.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope you can hear me now, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: It's running again. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your permission, I would like to proceed with my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would also like to use this break to make a remark to deal with the technical aspect of the presentation of this expert analysis, the expert analysis written by Mr. Vilicic on behalf of the Defence; namely, Mr. Vilicic will use the computer that he has in front of him to present certain parts of his expert's analysis to the Trial Chamber and everyone else in the courtroom in order to make it more graphic and easier to understand. The channel that will be used is marked as "computer monitor" or computer evidence" on the buttons that we have. I do wish to point out that it could happen that the image is not sharp enough on the monitors that we have in front of us. The technical staff have informed us that the only way to deal with this problem is for each individual monitor to have its image sharpened so that what Mr. Vilicic is about to present can be clearly seen. Therefore, if any problems should arise, they can be dealt with in that way. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, could I just mention something that does concern me. Counsel may have considered this, and they may see that there is no problem. But as I understand from what the professor has said, he uses as his fundamental source a statement given by General Marinovic to investigators of the Tribunal and evidence given by the general in the Milosevic trial. It may be, although it was not entirely clear, whether he has also relied on statements of other people such as Soldo given to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: These matters are not in evidence before this Trial Chamber. In other respects, the professor appears to have relied on material that was given in evidence before the Trial Chamber, and there is no problem about that. But to the extent that he has relied on material that isn't in evidence before us, it may prove to be a significant difficulty in the acceptance of his opinions. So I mention that at the outset so that both yourself and counsel for the Prosecutor can be considering this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. After consultation with my colleague, I will present the position of the Defence, and I will take this opportunity to take advantage of your proposal and I will consult this with my colleague from the OTP during the break. Of course, we gave this some thought, and I can later present my arguments of how and why this witness had relied on these sources that we have just cited in the introduction to his expert analysis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vilicic, according to the information that you had at the time while you were working on this expert report, what was the position of firing position of the JNA in the Dubrovnik battlefield?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: As you said, I would like to present to the Honourable Chamber by using slides, and we have prepared them for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: We have the slide on our monitor, so could you kindly --

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: Please follow this arrow that I'm going to point the firing position of the JNA with. Given the fact that the number of projectiles that landed inside the Old Town of Dubrovnik and judging by all relevant statements made by witnesses, those primarily involved were shells, mortar shells. Therefore, in our analysis, we focussed on the firing positions of mortar weapons of the Yugoslav People's Army. The first firing position was of the firing group of the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Brigade of Trebinje, and that was a 120-millimetre mortar position deployed in the sector Ledenice, in the proximity of the road leading to Ivanica. The next firing position of the organic composition of weaponry of the 3rd Battalion of mortars that were in the Dubac and Rajcevici sector, we called it the Rajcevic location. The next firing position involved mortars at Strincijera, six 82-millimetre mortars, 69A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. Is this map in evidence? And I don't see it in his materials, unless I'm misreading them, or it's an enlargement of one of the maps in his materials.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this map is part of the expert report at the very beginning. So most certainly, it is part of evidence. And that is my response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's not presently an exhibit, not a previous map we have.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, no, Your Honour. This map is an integral part of the expert report and an addendum thereto that had been submitted in accordance with the Rule 94 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Prosecution seem to be having trouble finding it, and no member of the Chamber has yet found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vilicic, would you please assist us and show us where exactly this map that we see on our screens is in the report.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: That's part of the map, 1 to 25.000 scale, Dubrovnik, as part of the addendum 1. And you also have an addendum 2 to the expert report where another part of this map is contained at a scale of 1 to 50.000 as opposed to a scale of 1 to 25.000. In the expert report, this map is on page of the English version -- if I may say, it's just one segment of the topographic map. We did not treat it as a separate map, but rather we used this in order to determine the coordinates of firing positions of the weaponry of the Yugoslav People's Army and the Dubrovnik Defence Forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Vilicic. Where is the map in the English version of the report?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: Figure 1B, I think, on page -- it is, in fact, part of the figure 1.1. The figure shows number 1.1, 82-millimetre firing positions, whereas here on the picture we only have firing positions indicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I hope we have clarified this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic. Two out of three have found it. That's a good start.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I apologise for this. It is quite clear that this is a huge document and that due to that, unfortunately, we may face certain problems and confusion. But quite simply, it's something that happens with such big volume of the material that you have in front of you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vilicic, before my learned colleague made an objection, you had shown us the firing positions in question. Can you just tell us briefly how did you mark each of these firing positions? Which symbols did you use?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: We marked firing positions by using the mark VP-1. That's the position of the 120-millimetre Ledenice mortar; VP-3 refers to the sector of Rajcevici; VP-4 is the position 82 millimetres in Strincijera; and on the monitor, you can see VP-2 firing position, which refers to anti-aircraft guns, so-called ZIS 70 that were attached to the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Motorised Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Which Croatian unit positions did you take into consideration? How did you mark those?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: I must say that we did not take into consideration the positions of Croatian forces, but rather we indicated their firing positions with letter C, in fact, of their firing pieces. This primarily refers to C-1, which indicates the position of the Croatian forces at Imperial fortress on Srdj; C-4 refers to 82-millimetre mortar positions deployed at 200 metres from the Old Town and from Ploce; C-5 refers to the weapons that were deployed to the north of the town based on the information that we heard from witness's testimonies; C-3 indicates the firing position of mortars that were in Bogosica Park; C-6 was a firing position at 500 metres from the Old Town. And in my further testimony, I will point out the relevance of selecting this particular firing position.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Are there any other targets that you have marked?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: C-7 was marked here because there was some talk about firing pieces at Gradac, and later on you will hear that it was along the line between C-3 and C-7 that could possibly be targeted from VP-1, and that is the target C-3 and 6 and 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In view of the firing positions of the JNA units that you have marked, can you tell us, please, how was it possible to direct fire from these JNA positions that, as I said, you indicated on the map?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: The deployment of firing positions of the JNA firing pieces that needed correction in observance and ranging could be done only from the main observation post at Zarkovica, only for correcting hits from VP-1 position of 120-millimetre mortars and 82-millimetre mortars from VP-3. The observation post at Zarkovica was not able to monitor and direct the fire of mortars positioned at Strincijera given the configuration of the terrain around it, and the impossibility of establishing a so-called parallel axis between this position and the range of targets, and that is the direction of observation and firing from Strincijera. For that reasons, the weapons from Strincijera could only fire on the basis of direct observations by the company commander deployed at Strincijera. If I made add one more thing, given the configuration of the terrain, it was very difficult to observe and to correct fire from Zarkovica for VP-1 and VP-2 firing position for the reasons that are evident from the map, and that is that there was a very huge so-called rear slope which indicates that at the impact of the projectile, the realistic dispersion is considerably higher than those in the table. And therefore, the estimate of those men directing fire from the observation post at Zarkovica was very difficult, or rather it was very inaccurate in this particular case.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us briefly, please, which kind of firing pieces did you take into consideration in your expert report?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: As I already said, given the nature of the projectiles that landed inside the walls of the Old Town, we were focussed mostly on mortars. Since according to the establishment, the 3rd Battalion had 82 and 120-millimetre mortars, we were primarily focussed on them. And as for firing support pieces, we analysed the positions and the possibility for firing from 130-millimetre guns given their extreme precision and well-known destructive power of those missiles fired from them. In addition, we showed in this sketch the firing position of 76-millimetre anti-armour guns that only could be used to target and neutralise C-1 firing position which was at Srdj, the imperial fortress where the Croatian forces were deployed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Let me now dwell on what is a theoretical part of your report where you have analysed and explained some basic terms that one needs to know in order to be able to comprehend the essence of your report. So I would like to ask you whether all fired projectiles hit the given target, or are there any deviations from the given objective or target?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: In principle, there is no single weapon that can always hit the one and the same point. In other words, it is only natural that during firing of any kind of projectile, there occurs a so-called dispersion, and that is the deviation of the projectile in respect to the targeted point.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, what are the two main reasons for this kind of deviation when the projectile hits?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: In addition to a series of reasons that may cause this and that we have explained in detail in this report, there are two main reasons, two main factors that considerably affect and produce deviation of the projectile from the desired target. First of all, that is the impact of the initial velocity of the projectile; and secondly, the influence or meteorological conditions, most of all the intensity and direction of winds. This particularly refers to mortar shells who are extremely sensitive to wind power because they're not stabilised by using a gyroscope and that is by revolving around their own axis; rather, they use flaps, small flaps which are also very sensitive to wind blows.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you mention some other causes that lead to dispersion.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: I have just given the technical aspect of the matter right now. However, if we look at the total dispersion of projectiles in real terms, we can subdivide this practically into three groups. One group are characteristics and the state of the weapon system. Secondly, it is the meteorological situation as I've already mentioned in which the firing takes place. And thirdly, it is the level of training and knowledge of the crews that are carrying out the preparation for the firing and who guide fire aimed at the target.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, please, is there a difference in dispersion if firing takes place from one weapon only or from several weapons?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That is the main shortcoming when analysing a system and its precision. If one does not take into account the existence of this particular difference involving one weapon or several weapons, especially if targeting a concentrated objective. That is to say, all weapons concentrate on one target. Since there cannot be technical equality in the performance of all weapons, each and every individual weapon has certain deviations, especially in terms of initial velocity as I've already said, and also there can be errors made by the crews manning each and every weapon. So this dispersion, when a group of weapons is firing, is manifested in terms of distance and in terms of the range. So if we look at the tables, there is an increase by 1 and a half up to 3 times all together. So when a group of artillery pieces is firing, if we only look at the dispersion presented at the -- in the tables, an error is made that is 1 and a half times up to 3 times greater than what the tables say. So actually, there is less dispersion than actually in reality.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you present this to us in graphic terms.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: Well, if we look at the next slide, we see what it's like when four mortars are firing. In our case, we have 120-millimetre mortars in the area of Ledenice. There were four that were in proper condition out of six. And also, there were four, and only on Strincijera there were six 82-millimetre mortars. We see here a schematic. We see how this is manifested in the field. That is to say, when the area is leveled, when the ground is level. We see how this dispersion is manifested. In the next table, you see how big the dispersion is in terms of range and direction. So if we carry out this adjustment according to the target, it can even go up to 2.2. And in terms of direction, it can even go up to 9 possible deviations because sighting equipment especially in mortars is very significant, but still they do not make it possible to precisely target a given objective with that weapon. So usually, a particular mortar uses a pole when targeting, and then that pole can indicate how big the error is. So the -- it increases with range. And of course, when the range is bigger, then the error is bigger, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, please, what is the influence of the slope of the terrain, flanking, rear slope, and so on?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: It is significant, especially of the so-called rear slope. This was already mentioned before this Honourable Trial Chamber. We have prepared a specific situation that had prevailed at Srdj where the facing slope was 15 to 20 degrees. As it was already said, dispersion of projectiles is reduced at the facing slope. And then the rear slope went even up to 48 degrees, meaning that dispersion was considerably increased; that is to say, that every projectile that would fall behind Srdj towards the Old Town down there, it would have greater dispersion in terms of range than the projectiles that fell in front of the Srdj fortress. And specifically, there was a flanking slope between 8 and 12 degrees. On the next slide --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please speak a bit slower, please.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: We can see the arithmetic involved on the next slide. Specifically for the 48-degree slope the probable dispersion in the tables is 31 metres, and in reality it is 106 metres on the ground. As for the flanking slope, it has relatively less of an effect. The left and the right one provide the same values in terms of the increase, and you can see down here that dispersion in terms of direction, the tables give 21, and it is only 26 metres in real terms. That is to say that the rear slope considerably increases the range dispersion, but not the direction dispersion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean when you say that, increased in terms of range?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: Well, if we are targeting an objective that is on the horizon, then of course, when one weapon is used for firing, then the dispersion picture is probably going to be 8 dispersions, 8 probable dispersions. I'm intentionally not saying which ones. However, if a target is on the rear slope, then in this specific case instead of 240 metres, the picture -- the pattern would be 800 metres. If the objectives would be on that slope, that rear slope, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: All right. All right. That's as far as slopes are concerned, facing slope, rear slope, flanking slope. But Mr. Vilicic, what is the effect of altitude of the firing position, higher altitude in relation to the objective or target that is engaged?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: That is where most errors are made. If the position is at a higher altitude than the target is, as was the case in Dubrovnik specifically, when mortars at firing positions VP-1, VP-3, and VP-4 were at a higher altitude, about 300 metres on average above the targets that were around the Old Town, because the altitude of the Old Town ranges -- is around 50 metres, but Bogosica Park is about 170 metres or 180 metres, and the Ledenice position is about 390 metres. So this difference was almost 300 metres. Now, how did it yield an effect in that respect? We are targeting an objective that is at a lower altitude, lower than the firing position. Then there certainly has to be an overreach, an overshoot. And then the so-called correction from the mountain tables have to be used. They show the extent to which the elevation of the mortar has to be increased - because the mortar has a particular type of trajectory - in order to reduce the range and to obtain the desired hit and the desired target. On the other hand, if we were to take into account elevation that is horizontal, then there would be a larger range, or rather we would have an overshoot yet again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but the interpreters simply cannot keep up with your rate of speaking. I know that you're wanting to tell us a lot, but you'll just have to try and slow your rate of speaking. This is interpreted into more than one language, and time must be allowed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vilicic, would you please clarify one point: You were talking about altitudes in the town of Dubrovnik. Can you please tell us carefully and slowly what the altitudes are of the Old Town, of Bogosica Park, what altitudes are there and what did you take into account?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: In annex 9(a) in the annex to the expert analysis, we said exactly what the altitudes are of the firing positions of all the weapons that were in the area of Dubrovnik. Specifically, the firing position of the 120-millimetre mortar was in the area of Ledenice, and it was at 335 metres. That was the altitude. The mortars at the firing position of VP-3 in the area of Rajcevici were at an altitude of 285 metres. Mortars at firing position VP-4 were at an altitude of 390 metres. The altitudes of the targets or objectives are the following: The fort, the basic objective where the mortars were faced was the fort at Srdj, that is, 403 metres is the altitude of that feature. Then the weapons that we looked at had the following positions: C-3, mortars in Bogosica Park are at an elevation of 50 metres; mortars towards Ploce are at 200 metres away from the Old Town, and they're at an altitude of 40 metres; then to the north of the Old Town, there is C-5, some weapons there, and it is at an altitude of 90 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: That's why I said during my remarks that the altitude difference was 300 metres between the firing positions of the mortars as compared to the firing positions of the Croatian Defence Forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we are moving on to the next subject. Those are mistakes, errors, in preparing firing. What are the main reasons for these errors in the preparation of firing and in actual firing?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: I have slowed down for the sake of the interpreters. The main causes for errors in the execution of fire, rather, the preparation of fire, are multifold. We explained this in detail in our expert analysis. Starting from errors in terms of establishing where the firing position of the weapon is and where the firing position of the objective is, and then on the basis of topographical maps depending on the size of the map or rather the scale of the map where this is being carried out, these errors vary. Specifically for 1 to 25.000-scale map, the mistake can be up to 25 metres which corresponds to 1 millimetre.
