So we are talking about a lack of familiarity with all the information involved in terms of initial velocity of weapons systems or projectiles, then differences in weight, all the way to the ballistic characteristics, the temperature of the gunpowder and weather conditions, the atmospheric pressure, the velocity and direction of wind and so on. So there either has to be a knowledge or a lack of knowledge of this information. And then accuracy depends on that. If one has all relevant information about the artillery pieces involved, about the ammunition, meteorology, so-called weather conditions, the information received from balloons, pilots, and signals are obtained which show the exact pressure, air pressure and velocity and direction of wind. I don't want to go into all the details, but a so-called ballistic wind is established, and then corrections are made on the basis of that. If we have all of that, then when preparing the initial data, so-called full preparation takes place.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: We've come to the question of preparation. Tell us, please, how does the preparation take place of initial data for firing?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: By way of appropriate calculations, by using various auxiliary methods. That is to say, the numbers in the firing tables, they are depicted graphically, and then on the basis of that certain parameters can be established in order to determine basic information for particular artillery pieces. That is to say, the elevation from which the firing should take place. Then appropriate calculations of all improvements and corrections, so that with the first projectiles or the first group of projectiles there would be as little dispersion or deviation as possible. If one does not have all this information or if one has them only partially and depending on the situation involved, that is to say, the situation in the battlefield, then the following two degrees of preparation, or levels of preparation; the so-called abbreviated preparation, and then there has to be an estimate. Or, for example, the measurement of the so-called ground wind. Then temperature, air temperature is estimated, and also air pressure is taken roughly. Then initial data are obtained according to the methodology of the so-called abbreviated preparation. However, if there isn't enough time for a transfer of fire from one firing position, from one target to another, for example, if the enemy begins to fire from a position where they were not firing from before, and for example, in our case, the mortars faced one target, were trained on one target, and there needed to be a quick transfer of fire to another target so they could be neutralised. In that case, in this short period of time, there would be no time to carry out preparation. And then you need to take into account rough estimates of range and parameters are taken accordingly. And this is the reason for high dispersion, high dispersion in terms of the projectiles falling far from their targets, their designated targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: This precisely would be my next question. What are the effects of these different forms or levels of preparation, if you can please explain and also show us on a diagram.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: In our expert analysis, we gave the exact data. We provided tables which we have already discussed, a tabular overview of deviations or probable deviations for each of these three different methods in relation to the probable deviations as stated in the firing tables. And then the numerical data are provided in a table -- I must have it here somewhere. Here we go. We can see on the monitor the probable errors in terms of range and deflection depending on the method which was used to calculate the initial firing data. The best results, that is, the lowest deviations, are obtained whenever the so-called full preparation can be applied and used for setting the initial firing data. Then the deviations are between 0.8 and 1.2 per cent in terms of the range. And in terms of deflection, between 3 and 5. In order to make this clear, if you have a range of 1.000 metres, 3 would mean 3 metres. In a range of 3.000 metres, we would have 9 metres instead. Therefore, the deflection would be measured in terms of metres. Here 1.2 for total deviation. As for the other two values given in this table, this is the mean value for the abbreviated preparation and for the simple preparation. As you can see, the error in terms of range would be between 8 and 10 per cent. In that case, for simple preparation. In terms of deflection, between 20 and 30. On a range of 3.000 metres, this would amount to a 90-metre error.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Vilicic. Can you please now tell us about the meteorological parameters that might cause dispersion. Which are the relevant factors and how do they bear on dispersion or deviations in general.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: The three fundamental factors, meteorological factors, that are taken into account when you calculate the initial firing data and when you set the general data for firing are the atmospheric air pressure, the air temperature, and the wind. If you look at these three factors, that having the greatest effect on dispersion is the wind. The wind has two components: One is facing wind, wind against the direction of firing; and the other component is a crosswind which causes the projectile to be deflected, and that is the so-called lateral or crosswind.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In your calculations which we are about to go through, did you take into account the weather conditions in the Dubrovnik area at the time under consideration?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: We didn't have the precise data for the 6th of December, which is the day that we focussed on. However, in order to really be able to discuss and have a more general analysis, we consulted data that we obtained from the hydro-meteorological institute of the navy which used to be based in Split. They took an average of mean values over a period of 10 years in relation to the intensity and direction of the wind. They provided the wind roses for the entire Adriatic. And we studied the wind rose in relation to Dubrovnik, since it was the 6th of December, we studied the wind rose that related to December 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you point us to a graph or a diagram that shows that, please.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. If you look at this slide, you can see the wind rose for December in Dubrovnik. This is the one I'm talking about. This is where Dubrovnik is, and this is the so-called wind rose. This is north, and the vertical line marks northeast. This is the main direction in which a wind usually called Bura was blowing. It's a gale-force wind. Based on this wind rose and based on the methodology used to mark it on the map, you can see this line right here. And in order to determine its magnitude, here we have a scale, by measuring you can calculate the frequency of the wind of Bura in terms of percentage for the month of December. You use the length of this line. Specifically in relation to Dubrovnik, you can see it was 36 per cent. That was the frequency of wind in the month of December over a period of more than ten days on average. That is how often Bura occurs in Dubrovnik in the month of December on average. As for the wind's intensity, it is marked with these small lines, notches, notches. Specifically in relation to Dubrovnik, we can see four of those, and each of the notches is used to denote one degree, one on the Bofor scale. Therefore, the average velocity of the Bura wind in the Dubrovnik area in the month of December would be 4 on the Bofor scale. Later I will show you the proportion between the wind velocity as expressed on the Bofor scale in metres per second. I think that's about 8 metres per second. We shall see that later on. May I just be allowed to say something else in relation to this: In order to be able to understand what this is really about, in order to be able to understand what this means in practical terms, this velocity of the wind, you have the international standards and parameters in the next table. And correlations were given between the strength of wind in terms of the Bofor scale and metres per second. Specifically, in relation to Dubrovnik, the average, the mean value, was 4 on the Bofor scale. That means between 5.5 and 7.9 metres per second. However, you may notice how this is manifested on the surrounding environment where you have this strong gale-force wind. If you can see large tree branches moving, that usually is consistent with a Bura wind that is about 6 strong on the Bofor wind which means between 10.8 and 13.8 metres per second. We used video footage that was provided to us by the OTP, and we noticed that on account of this strong Bura wind that was blowing on the day, and also based on Djelo Jusic's testimony before this Tribunal, on that day, the famous Dubrovnik Bura wind was blowing, and the conclusion was that it had to be at least 6 on the Bofor scale. In order to further assess the strength of the wind, we used 10 metres per second. And throughout our expert analysis, the assumption was that the velocity of the wind on that day was 10 metres per second.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Vilicic, further in relation to the weather conditions, as far as you know, based on such facts as you have been able to review in the process of drafting this expert analysis, what about JNA units's positions in this area? Were radio probes used to carry out measurements in this area?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: No. All the equipment that we had in that room, the central room, because the infantry battalion was in direct contact with the Croatian forces near Dubrovnik, those units did not have such equipment in order to carry out measurements by radio probes. Usually, you had this sort of equipment at the corps level or at the level of a division in an area where combat operations are afoot. However, only on the condition that significant artillery pieces are present in the area that are about to launch important operations. As for our mortars that are under consideration here, these conditions were not in place. Our estimate is that there was no way for the initial preparation of -- for the full preparation of initial firing data to be carried out primarily because the lay of the land, the configuration of the terrain, and the relationship between the altitude of the weapons and the altitude of the targets was significant, significantly different. It was -- the difference was huge. And this made it impossible to have accurate calculations. First of all, there was no way to calculate the range because the lay of the land made it impossible to calculate exactly the mortar positions in relation to the designated targets. There was also the laser method of determining the range in relation to a target, and this was also impossible under these conditions. It couldn't be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Just two further questions in relation to this general background: What are the tabular values that we are talking about, and how exactly are they determined?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: As I've said before this Trial Chamber before, I was the chief of ballistics, and I was in charge of research. I was in charge of drawing up these firing tables for practically all the different weapons systems that the JNA had. The firing table is made using a certain methodology. You have target practices on a firing range. And you have all the information that you need in relation to weapons, projectiles, weather conditions, under certain kind of weather conditions, not just any kind of weather conditions. There are certain limits as to the temperature, the strength of the wind, and the crews are professionally trained crews, trained on a daily basis. And these tests are done at our testing range in Nikinci, so the obtained tabular values show a mean value that is typical of a certain system. However, these values are not maximum values, but rather mean values or average values as I've said. In relation to mortar ammunition, there is something called a standard of All People's Defence, 2369, which was published in 1984 according to which mortar ammunition is received or accepted. When you have these tests at a firing range, when you know everything about the weather conditions, when you have all the information on the weapons systems being used, when you have all possible information on the types of projectiles being used, the temperature, their eccentricity, their centre of gravity and so on and so forth, under such conditions, the dispersion for certain groups is allowed to be up to 1.5 times their tabular value. If during tests, between 15 and 20 consecutive series are fired, and then it is established that the mean value is higher than that originally defined in a table, this new mean value is multiplied by 1.5, and then series of mortar projectiles can be accepted. Also if, for example, during production it was increased from 1 to 1.2 in relation to the tabular value, this is then multiplied by 7 or 7.5 and the allowed dispersion value is between 1 and 1.8 times that given in the table.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may just ask another question from this area before the break, I would just like to ask Mr. Vilicic something else briefly with your permission.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vilicic, please, just briefly: Are there any differences between realtime situations and tabular values, values given in a table?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: Yes, there are essential differences. And it is impossible to look at the tabular values of possible dispersion and provide some sort of final evaluation of what dispersion values might be of a certain weapons system or artillery weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I propose that now we take a break as planned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic. We will resume at just after quarter to 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vilicic, I would now kindly ask you to discuss with us the chapter 4 of your expert report. And after that, I will ask you individual questions regarding what I believe is to be of relevance to be heard before this Honourable Trial Chamber. First of all, can you tell us, please, if we have this specific situation in mind, and that is the situation prevailing on the 6th of December 1991, how was it possible to carry out preparation of firing elements, and what methods were possible to be applied under such circumstances according to the information that you had at your disposal while you were writing this report?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: First we have to distinguish two different scenarios. The first scenario involves the primary target of mortars VP-4, VP-3, and VP-1, directed at the fortress at Srdj as a primary target of the attack by infantry units of the 3rd Battalion for rendering firing support to this attack. Under such circumstances, the preparatory works could have been done according to the so-called abbreviated method. In other words, they were able to assess the temperature, and by the way, it was an extremely cold day. They could have measured the ground wind. And since Srdj was -- as a target was clearly visible from all firing positions, they were able to establish accurately the direction and the distance to the target. In other words, without complete meteorological data, they were able to apply the so-called abbreviated method of preparing initial firing elements for offering firing support. The second aspect of this entire situation refers to the moment when mortars changed their primary azimuth directions because according to their performance, according to the structure, if they are aiming at Srdj without changing firing positions, they would not have been able to aim at other targets. And by that, I specifically refer to C-4, C-3, and C-5 targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please just explain to us what kind of changes does this involve.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: That is exactly what I was about to say. That means changes at the firing position. Mortars have certain structural angles they can move to the right or to the left from their primary direction. And to aim at this target, they had to move their bipod, and by changing their position upon which the barrels actually lean and which serve as a basis for determining the angle and the accuracy of the direction, they had to be, so to say, they had to disturb so to say all their basic parameters and to take a totally different direction and thereby automatically come to a position to renew the establishment of all parameters. I presume that under the conditions when an extremely heavy mortar fire came from the Croatian forces, and when the units of the 3rd Battalion found themselves in a position to be annihilated while attacking Srdj, they had urgently to effect counterbattery fire from mortars. But it wasn't done as in military terms would have been normal with artillery pieces; instead, they had to swiftly change the direction of fire to Srdj for a firing position of the Croatian forces in order to destroy them. Under such conditions, they could fire only from the so-called -- by using the so-called simple elements of firing or by using the so-called simple method of preparations which required very quick assessment of the range, of the direction, and by firing not only from one but from the battery of weapons in order to engage the target and to eliminate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So what kind of effect does this situation produce?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: This situation probably led to the fact that a number of projectiles did fall inside the walls of the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What you explained during the last few minutes is that the first segment of firing, according to the knowledge that you have, they applied the so-called abbreviated preparations, and the second segment involves the so-called simple preparation.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: Objectively, there was no conditions granting for preparation. I apologise. I didn't give you an answer how we approach this in our analysis. We took into consideration both the simple and the abbreviated method of preparation in order to make certain comparisons and to see what effect this may have produced, I mean negative effects in this specific instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let us now move on to the ballistic analysis of firing from individual firing positions of JNA at specific targets. First of all, by following the sequence that you used in your analysis, I would like to ask you to analyse fire opened from the firing position VP-1 targeting the objectives marked C-3 and C-4. Can you please explain what kind of conclusions you reach in this particular segment.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: Let us first look into the fire from 120-millimetre mortars positioned in the Ledenice sector at the VP-1 firing position. The fire opened from these mortars at C-3 target. The first group of mortars -- of Croatian forces in Bogosica Park, then the target of another group of mortars which were positioned about 200 metres east was Ploce, and the firing pieces positioned at 100 metres to the north from the Old Town walls. On this slide, you can see the primary direction. This is the firing position. So this blue line indicates the primary direction of mortar fire in concentrated fire targeting C-3. The red lines on the right and on the left indicate possible deviation of the direction allowed by the structural features of each mortar. It is -- our presumption was that they were all concentrated on C-3, and they can only deviate as much to the left or to the right. As you can see, when directing fire in counterbattery fire against the Croatian mortars positioned in the Bogosica Park, the sector of the possible fire of mortars does not encompass the Old Town of Dubrovnik. On the next slide, we can see this big rectangular with lateral and vertical lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting you, but for the sake of clarity, could you please take the English version of your expert paper, and let us find this drawing in the English version. As I understand, this is the sketch on page 50, item 4.3. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: No. In the English version, it's on page 52, item 4.4.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Tell us about this sketch.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: This is the figure 4.4 on page 52.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: In this rectangular, I don't know if you can see it clearly, is an area where the first projectiles would have fallen had they been fired in the direction of Bogosica Park under the so-called simple preparation. In other words, it could be expected that a projectile may land even here, which is considerably in front of the target, or at the target itself, or far from the target on the other side. What does this practically mean? This means that there was an enormous dispersion and inaccuracy of hits with the elements contained in the simple preparation for this firing at C-3 target in Bogosica Park. On the same slide, we can see this smaller rectangular painted yellow, and the target centre is marked with a red point. And this is the dispersion pattern that would have occurred after the so-called correction of fire and after the firing of hits. Now, concerning the correction, I have to say the following --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Let us please focus on this figure.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: In circumstances when there are no appropriate conditions for valid observation and when we made swift estimates of initial firing elements or data, I said that the correction is in principle, and if you have ample time, is done by one weapon, and that is the so-called primary weapon. However, if a unit finds itself in a critical situation under heavy fire, then correction can be done through battery firing. Two or four mortars fire simultaneously. By observing the purpose of the hit, and that is whether one or several hits fell short or behind the target, and then so-called command for correction is made by either reducing or increasing the range. While this kind of correction is in progress, and if you have four mortars firing, and if four shells are fired, and then the next four follow, it is only logical that within this rectangular, these 4, 8, or probably 12 shells will land within this rectangular for as long as they manage to achieve the so-called rule of fork, and at least three groups of weapons which means at least 12 shells have to be fired before we approximate the target or the mean hit. If that is achieved, then with such element, if we proceed to fire, the shells would continue to fall within this yellow rectangular -- rectangle. And as we can see in this specific case, none of the shells would land inside the Old Town of Dubrovnik. In the first scenario before we did the correction, as you can see from this diagram which was made at 1 to 25.000 scale, we have plotted here the Old Town, it is evident that the pattern of simple preparation covers the Old Town with a 20 per cent of probability. In other words, there is a high level of probability that out of the 12 shells, a number of them could even fall in the Old Town, even though the Old Town was not the target of operation in this particular instance. This only under the condition that the mean hit strikes the target that we have this level of dispersion, and that around the target we have the pattern of dispersion. Of course, again, under the condition that the wind velocity is practically zero. If in this concrete situation, when on the 6th of December there was an extremely strong Bura wind in Dubrovnik, and if we take it as an assumption that it was blowing latitudinally, we can find where the certain hits would land despite the correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, in the English version of your report, where is the situation that you're describing right now?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: This situation is not described in the English version. There is figure 4.41 in the English version which was drafted for the condition that shells had been exposed to the lateral wind blowing 10 metres per second.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you please explain the lateral wind.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: So if the projectile was exposed to a lateral wind, then in that case some of them will start to fall within the red area on the diagram. However, if they're exposed to lateral wind, then they will start to fall also within the green area. In other words, the yellow rectangle will basically remain where it is, or it will be shifted slightly. However, other projectiles will also start to fall either in the red or in the green area depending on the direction of wind. It is well known that the Bura wind is a shifting wind, that it blows in gusts which means that for the flight of a projectile, it blows differently which means that at one point it can achieve its maximum value, whereas at another point in time it can slow down. The correction that I explained which takes into account wind velocity and effects, once the velocity drops, the projectile fired at that very moment will fall at a -- at a completely different distance than originally calculated with the wind factor. That was the main reason why under such unfavourable weather conditions as was the case on the 6th of December in Dubrovnik we have an extremely increased dispersion pattern or a very, very low rate of accuracy of hitting the target, which means that this enormous dispersion, both along the range and direction --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you please focus directly on specific firing position and specific targets.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: That's what I'm talking about, Mr. Petrovic. Based on that, and on this conclusion that I just explained, this pattern is fully realistic because the entire rectangle composed of the yellow, the red, and the green areas becomes the image of the dispersion pattern under given conditions. Of course, under the presumption that there was no error in the estimate. The following slide shows the same objective or target, but under the condition that an error in the estimate of the direction occurred, 1-degree error equals 16.71 thousandths part which in this 5.700 range, 100 metres will be the deviation from the mean direction as opposed to the originally desired one if an error is only 1 degree, and it is very much relevant because the 120-millimetre mortar firing group was physically unable to see the target and to orient themselves according to it, but they rather had to use some provisional segments in order to direct the fire. We can see in this slide that even if you apply an abbreviated method of preparations, the projectiles during the correction in the course of firing with the shorter or a longer range, the projectiles may fall -- may have fallen inside the Old Town. And what is characteristic about this situation is that this involved the northern and the western part of the town. Now, for example, can I just proceed now. Can I just finish with this. Now, there is the following case: If we look at the original picture, if everything that I spoke of so far was done with an error of 1 degree in terms of direction, so 1 degree was the mistake in direction, and they went left in relation to the objective, you can see that although the correction was made, due to the effect of the wind, a number of projectiles can fall into the Old Town. Can you see this? Can you see where the arrow is, the part of the Old Town that is already affected? And finally, we wanted to show, since this was objectively speaking simple preparation, and we could see from the table that the margin of error can be 8 to 10 per cent, this entire dispersion with an error of 8 to 10 per cent due to the effect of the wind, it completely covers this northwestern part of town. In this situation, it is only logical, regrettably, that some projectiles fell into the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Have we dealt with it now?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: On this slide, you can see how the Old Town was affected. You see that it is enlarged now. So the Pile gate is affected, and also it goes through that entrance into the Old Town. This entire area, that is. This is the Franciscan monastery there? I think the monastery is where the tower is, the one that can be seen on some pictures, the one that was hit. And then there is Bokara, the tower of Bokar, all of that is in the shadow if I can put it that way of these possible impacts in the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Before we move on, could you please mark in the English version of your expert opinion the diagrams that this pertains to so that it would be easier to follow what you have been telling us.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, we thought the expert opinion was enormous anyway, and we thought it would be way too big if we were to include all these pictures. We just gave these two pictures, that is to say, figure 4.4 constitutes the dispersion of hits with simple preparation without the effect of the wind on page 52. And 4.41 is dispersion not only after simple preparation, but also under the influence of the wind at 10 metres per second when as I said there is this gust of wind, as I said. So you can see that this point of the rectangle touches this left part of the Old Town. This can clearly be seen on the previous slide. It fully corresponds to this slide. I'm going to show it to you right now. You see, it fully corresponds to the slide except that the upper part is not there, only the yellow part. That is the effect of the lateral wind. Then there's this yellow rectangle. Now imagine that it went down and that it was here, that this point of it is down here. So we have presented this graphically so that it would be easier for you to visualise what the effect of the lateral wind is in this specific case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, sorry to interrupt, Your Honour. We don't have a 4.4 on page 52. We have a 4.13 on that page. And we don't have a 4.41 in the document that we were provided with. Is it in the addendum?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, below the figure, it says figure 4.4 on page 52. So we are talking about figures. We are talking about diagrams, pictures.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I see. I'm looking at the 4.13 on the top. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vilicic --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, actually, may I proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vilicic, we spoke about VP-1 firing at C-3.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could we please focus at VP-1 firing at C-4 now.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: Here we are. On this slide, we can see on this slide -- this is 4.45. That's what we're talking about. And it involves abbreviated preparations, and we see what the dispersion was in the preparation. So we're talking about abbreviated preparation. And after the correction, the dispersion of the projectile on the assumption that the median hit was close to the target, but either left, right, up, or down. The table that is provided here, the one that you see here, up here, shows how many projectiles out of 100 projectiles fired fall within each and every one of these fields of the yellow rectangle. So for example, if we look at this red point, these two fields, left and right, these two fields, when 100 projectiles are fired, the average that is taken, of course, is that 6 projectiles fall within these four fields. So if these four fields were to cover the target or the Old Town, there would be a total of 23 projectiles that would fall. According to this methodology, because the central part does not cover the Old Town, but this is a field of probability, 2, 7, and partly 16 per cent, so these are the ones we're talking about. Our rough estimate was that these 4 plus 4 equals 8, plus 2, 10, plus 2, 12, that 12 projectiles after firing correction; that is to say, after fire is opened at C-4, they fall into the Old Town according to all the laws of the theory of probability and dispersion rules. So the conclusion we draw is that this firing position, or rather target, in fact, by its very position imperilled the Old Town of Dubrovnik because neutralising that target meant that necessarily a certain number of projectiles would have to fall within the Old Town of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Just tell us in the English version, where can we find this diagram.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: This is 4.5 on page 54 of the English version. Figure 4.5. [In English] Page 54.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, please go on.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: The same analysis like in the previous case: There was no impact of the wind. However, since the Bura blows in gusts of varying intensity along the trajectory of the projectile, the projectile would fall into the red zone as well. If the projectiles would be subjected to a lateral wind, then they would start falling within the green area, too. Fortunately, this green area as you can see here is outside the Old Town, so the projectiles would fall into the sea. While the previous picture, or rather the red area shows that the number of projectiles that would fall into the Old Town would be increased. In other words, I can say that the objective, or rather the firing position C-4 of the second group of the mortars of the Croatian forces posed a threat to the Old Town in view of their vicinity. So when the JNA weapons counterfire, projectiles may fall into the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: Let me just show you what this looks like when it's enlarged. You can see the area of the Old Town that is affected by normal dispersion after corrections; that is to say, part of the Old Town of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: VP-1 and C-4, is there anything else you would like to say in relation to that or should we move on to the next firing position?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: We can move on to the next firing position. I think this is evident. I think that the graph shows that the Old Town of Dubrovnik was seriously jeopardised when there was a firing position only 200 metres away from Ploce. Now, on this slide, you see the position that was discussed before this Honourable Trial Chamber. I was present during the testimony of one witness here. The position of the anti-aircraft gun that was 100 metres to the north of the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So that is the position -- that is --

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: This is position C-5, C-5.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What kind of results did you obtain in relation to that position?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: Well, take a look at it. I think it is self-explanatory. According to abbreviated preparations and upon corrections, that is to say with a higher degree of probability of hitting the objective, the Old Town of Dubrovnik is practically completely covered, or rather jeopardised. So projectiles can fall into it. A number of projectiles had to fall within the Old Town when mortars fire. And now, when correction is carried out, it can be seen clearly that the northwest part of the Old Town is fully covered with the dispersion pattern of 120-millimetre mortar, and all those indicators show that that is where most of the shells fell. And that's where most of the damage was occurred, according to all reports received.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at the English version of your report, and could you tell us what page this is and what figure number you have referred to just now.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, this is in a special chapter.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The page is 77, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's right. This is a special chapter, page 77, figure 21.1. It says "Slika" in the Serbian language, but figure 21.1 would be the English equivalent. Page 77.

utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, since at this point in time we would have to move on to another firing position, I would suggest that we adjourn for the day and continue working tomorrow.

utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic. I think that's a logical place to break. Now, to avoid any confusion, we will be resuming tomorrow at 9.30.
